# Behavioral Neuroscience 392: course-specific lecture rules

These instructions apply ONLY to this course. The instructor’s request takes precedence over inherited Neuroethology rules. This is the connected BEHAVNEUR-392- GitHub repository at https://github.com/jordanxxlopez/BEHAVNEUR-392-.git. Keep all Behavioral Neuroscience materials in this repository, separate from NEUR 411.

## Deliverables and level

Build 19 chapter PowerPoints, one per verified chapter in Carlson and Birkett, Physiology of Behavior, Global Edition, 13th edition (2022), ISBN 9781292430256. Verify the table of contents before recording chapter mapping. The instructor explicitly requests descriptive lecture titles, not "Chapter 1"; use the authorized topic title in course/schedule.json. Start with Chapter 1 unless directed otherwise. Prefer 75 slides total: 1 title, 73 content, 1 final Key takeaways. Expand only when useful, to at most 85 total. Do not invent a timetable. Each chapter may span several class meetings.

This is an undergraduate Behavioral Neuroscience course, easier than NEUR 411 but intellectually demanding. Define terms at first use. Explain neuronal signaling, pathways, experimental manipulations, and behavioral findings through direct, concrete teaching sentences. Introduce unfamiliar machinery in steps; avoid graduate-level prerequisite knowledge.

## Teaching prose and transcript requirements: all chapters

Follow [course/TEACHING_STYLE.md](course/TEACHING_STYLE.md) for every chapter, every slide paragraph, and every speaker-note teaching transcript, including authorized revisions. The instructor rejected generic research-summary prose in Chapter 4 and supplied a preferred plain-language rewrite. Match that example's connected explanatory sentences, definitions woven into the prose, and clear descriptions of what changes in the cell. Teach the actual biology: identify the relevant molecule or structure, explain what it does, specify what changes, and describe the resulting cellular or behavioral response. Define unfamiliar machinery in ordinary language as it is introduced. Explain the action behind phrases such as "recruits intracellular signaling" or "changes cellular function" without replacing them with a dense chain of unexplained protein names.

Every paragraph, including paragraph three, adds substantive information from the sources. Do not close with a statement about what the study brings together, places in a broader context, illustrates, highlights, connects, or teaches. Do not replace explanation with "access, target location, and cellular machinery all matter" or another obvious list of factors. State the specific transport process, receptor location, signaling step, time-dependent change, inhibitor result, anatomy, or behavioral finding instead. A correct but empty summary is still unacceptable.

Read each slide and transcript aloud as a professor explaining the material. Sentences must develop one another, not stack unexplained technical names or repeat the title. Apply the deletion test: if a sentence can disappear without losing a definition, mechanism, source-specific finding, experimental detail, or necessary scientific distinction, remove or replace it. A plain-language conclusion is welcome when it explains the biological change, as in the instructor's supplied example. A regex pass is not a teaching-quality pass. Review the third paragraph separately for generic wrap-up language. Keep this course's 5–7 rendered lines per paragraph; never import Neuroethology's older sentence quota or pad a paragraph to satisfy length. For the current Chapter 4 revision, replace only the three content paragraphs and matching teaching transcripts. Preserve all titles, slide order, layout, figures, recordings, captions, credits, and takeaways.

## Teaching and balance

Use 30–40% textbook foundations and 60–70% primary-research teaching, adjusted to the chapter. At the preferred count, 29 foundation slides and 44 research slides give approximately 40%/60%. Foundation slides teach mechanisms from the textbook even when an existing study figure illustrates the concept; retagging alone is insufficient. Tag each content slide instructional_role as foundation or research; do not count an incidental citation as research teaching. The textbook defines chapter scope and concepts. Interweave concept teaching with directly related primary studies rather than separating a foundation block from a research block. Connect studies to the topic and mechanism just introduced; emphasize current research while revisiting essential older work. Never say "the textbook" or add textbook metacommentary in visible teaching prose. References and source-image credits still identify the textbook accurately. Review every video and added image for its relationship to the adjacent concept, not merely its availability. Teach each concept, then use source-supported study findings to explain how it works. Use a manageable group of core papers across several slides rather than a different paper on every slide. Include current accessible research and foundational work where needed; verify references and quantitative claims.

Every paragraph teaches material. Use direct, concrete teaching sentences in three paragraphs. Each content paragraph must occupy 5–7 full rendered lines, checked against the exported PDF. Expand explanations rather than add filler, forced line breaks, or blank-line padding. The line requirement supersedes the earlier 70–110-word target. Identify the actor, action, and result. Do not summarize with vague verbs such as connected, linked, supported, or relationship. For example: "The neurons move the paddle. A hit or miss determines the electrical signal sent back to them." Scientific connections can still be described literally when their anatomy is the subject. Use three substantive paragraphs per content slide and natural complete-sentence teaching transcripts in notes, adapting depth to this easier class and readable layout. Do not pad paragraphs to meet a sentence count. No agendas, learning objectives, previews, fixed method-result-limitation templates, presentation commentary, or em dashes in visible text. Do not end paragraphs on routine limitations or stock caution. The instructor will discuss limitations and the importance of controls orally. Preserve scientifically necessary distinctions and genuine experimental conditions; do not turn hypotheses into facts. No p-values, error bars quoted in prose, test names, or sample-size bookkeeping. Retain quantities that explain the concept. Finish with 5–6 exam-level takeaways with bold lead phrases.

## Format

16:9, Arial throughout. Preserve the Neuroethology content-slide style. For this course’s TITLE SLIDE ONLY: white background, a large credited source image on the LEFT, and the instructor-approved descriptive lecture title, course/date, Jordan Lopez, Ph.D., and Professor of Neurobiology & Biomedical Engineering on the RIGHT. Do not mirror or recolor the source image. Body text/captions/footers black; titles and bold words use the chapter’s coordinated restrained theme. Separate theme ledger from NEUR 411; no yellow, orange, gold, purple, or green. Record themes after final validation. Never copy the former professor’s slide style. Analyze their slides for existing course coverage only when available.

## Figures

Every content slide has a relevant source image. Preserve existing intact study panels. Add a few original credited cell, anatomy, animal, or apparatus photographs where these make the slide concept recognizable. Fit images and movies without changing source aspect ratios or making scientific panels illegible. Prioritize intact primary-article panels. Textbook crops are explicitly allowed for foundations: retain original labels, caption Carlson and Birkett (2022), figure number and printed page, and record PDF page, ISBN, edition, and source. Retain enough context for students to interpret axes, labels, units, and scale bars. Never generate, redraw, replot, recolor, or reconstruct any scientific image, diagram, chart, or animation. Up to 10 genuinely useful credited web images are permitted. Give the full source reference in notes. New crops are made with tools/crop_figure.py; record crop boxes. Do not post the full uploaded textbook to GitHub.

## Videos

For Chapter 2 and subsequent new chapter decks, require exactly 20 distinct useful academic videos PLUS 20 distinct aesthetic animal/neuroscience recordings, totaling 40 embedded videos. This instructor update supersedes the former 20–30-video range. Existing Chapter 1 deliveries retain their recorded media counts unless a revision is requested. Choose each recording for its adjacent concept; do not reuse unrelated repository footage merely because it is available. For Chapter 3 onward, distribute all 40 recordings across the entire content sequence: 10 in each consecutive quarter, no gap greater than three content slides, and at least five in the final ten content slides. Never put media-purpose labels such as aesthetic, academic recording, or context video in visible slide text, captions, titles, or teaching notes. Keep these classifications only in the media manifest. Spread them through the material where appropriate; preserve article figures on video slides. Academic web/YouTube recordings by primary researchers and labs are permitted even when not publisher supplementary movies. No news reports, shorts, TikTok-style edits, unrelated entertainment, or fabricated scenes. Verify and accurately credit source authors, original URLs, study DOI when associated, and supplied license. Aesthetic recordings are real footage connected to the chapter, credited, with their purpose classified in internal records only, and never counted as primary scientific evidence or toward the academic-video quota. User uploads remain uploads, not fabricated article supplements.

Embed PowerPoint-compatible MP4s. Preserve native resolution, timing, audio, aspect ratio, and scientific scenes. Compress only when necessary and verify quality. Record video purpose (academic/aesthetic), slide, source, DOI if applicable, dimensions, duration, audio, codec, and SHA256. Verify every embedded media relationship and all source hashes; do not count duplicate excerpts as different studies or pad with repetitions. Retain static source posters. Report untested desktop playback honestly.

## Access

If a paper is blocked, find an accessible primary paper teaching the same necessary concept. Request the paper upload only if that particular source is indispensable. If a selected necessary VIDEO is blocked, stop final delivery and give an exact numbered upload list with original URL, source/paper DOI, movie identifier, and teaching purpose. Continue independent preparation. Never claim an inaccessible PDF, book, prior deck, or video was reviewed. The full book was too large to transfer, but all six split PDFs have now been downloaded. The contents and Introduction chapter were read directly; keep the full source PDFs private and ignored.

# Teaching prose and speaker transcripts

This instructor correction applies to all Behavioral Neuroscience chapters and authorized revisions. It applies equally to visible slide text and the teaching transcript before References in speaker notes. Source credits and original figure legends retain their source wording.

Teach the mechanism, anatomy, physiology, and behavior directly, at the plain-language level of the instructor's supplied cannabinoid rewrite below. Use connected explanations, definitions woven into the prose, and clear descriptions of what changes in the cell. A slide should leave the student able to explain a specific biological process, not merely repeat that a study examined it. Do not replace vague prose with a dense list of technical proteins or experimental abbreviations.

- Name the actor and explain its action. For example, myosin uses ATP to generate force against actin; it does not merely "recruit cellular machinery."
- Define a technical term where students first need it. An enzyme is not explained by naming several other enzymes. Introduce the relevant structure, action, and consequence in ordinary language.
- Explain intermediate steps when the sources establish them. State where a compound enters, which receptor it reaches, what the receptor changes, and how the measured response changes. Do not fill a gap in the evidence with an invented pathway.
- Use source-specific findings: which cell or animal, what treatment or manipulation, what changed, and in which direction. Explain an inhibitor by naming the step it blocks and the response that persists or disappears.
- Each paragraph adds information. Paragraph three may teach a further mechanism, a different condition, a follow-up result, or a relevant anatomical or behavioral detail. It has no fixed closing function.
- Retain a conclusion when it makes a concrete biological claim supported by the preceding evidence. Delete conclusions that merely praise the experiment, announce a connection, or say that several factors matter.
- Write connected sentences that sound natural aloud. Avoid both dense strings of unexplained terms and choppy lists of obvious facts. Do not add a fixed number of sentences.
- Preserve scientifically necessary distinctions, including hypothesis versus result, cultured cells versus intact animals, and calcium fluorescence versus transmitter release. State the distinction within the explanation rather than adding a stock caution paragraph.

Apply this deletion test to every sentence: would its removal lose a definition, mechanism, specific finding, experimental detail, or necessary scientific distinction? If not, delete or replace it. Apply the test separately to every final paragraph. Automated wording checks catch recurring failures; they do not assess scientific depth.

## Rejected wording

"The study brings drug action back to a complete causal sequence: a compound reaches a receptor, the receptor recruits intracellular signaling, effectors alter cellular function, and the changed cell contributes to a larger neural system."

This does not explain the CB1 signaling pathway, force generation, dendritic response, or the inhibitor results. Other unacceptable substitutes include "the findings place the mechanism in a broader context," "the experiment highlights the importance of cellular machinery," and "access and target location all matter."

## Instructor's preferred example

Cannabinoids can change the shape of neurons by activating CB1 receptors, which trigger signals inside the cell that affect its structure. In this study, researchers examined hippocampal neurons grown in a laboratory and observed changes in the cell body and dendrites, the branches that receive signals from other neurons. Together, these structures make up the somatodendritic region, so the findings showed that cannabinoid effects extended beyond the growing tip of the axon to other parts of the neuron.

These structural changes involve actin, a protein that forms part of the cytoskeleton, which is the internal framework that supports the cell and helps it change shape. When CB1 receptors are activated, signals inside the neuron can change how actin is organized, allowing the cell body and dendrites to change their shape. The images follow the same neuron over several minutes, allowing us to compare its appearance before and after receptor activation and see how its structure changes over time.

The length of receptor activation is important because changes in shape that happen within minutes are different from changes in growth or organization that develop after longer exposure. Researchers examined these effects separately to distinguish the neuron's immediate response from changes that emerge over time. This study shows how a chemical acting on a receptor can produce a physical change in a neuron by triggering signals that reorganize its internal framework and alter the shape of its cell body and dendrites.

Source: Roland et al. (2014), Figure 7. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.03159.

This example is the instructor's style reference, not a requirement to use these exact sentence lengths or a template for every slide. Maintain three paragraphs and the course's rendered-line requirement. Meaningful references to a recorded change or a concrete biological conclusion are allowed; empty statements about a study's importance are not.

Make Chapter [N] for Behavioral Neuroscience 392 as a downloadable editable PPTX. Follow this repository’s AGENTS.md and course/policy.json, using the instructor-approved descriptive lecture title and the verified chapter mapping from Carlson and Birkett (2022), Physiology of Behavior, Global Edition, 13th edition. Prefer 75 slides total, at most 85: one white title slide with source image left and instructor details right, substantive teaching content, and final Key takeaways. Use 30–40% textbook foundations and 60–70% primary-research teaching, adjusted to the chapter. Interweave each concept with directly relevant current and essential older studies; do not put all foundations first. Never say "the textbook" in teaching prose. Use short concrete sentences identifying who or what acts, what changes, and the measured outcome; avoid vague summaries using connected, linked, supported, or relationship. Use three teaching paragraphs, each with 5–7 actual rendered lines. Expand the mechanism and behavioral explanation with direct sentences, not filler or vague prose. Check every paragraph after PDF export. Define concepts for an undergraduate course easier than NEUR 411. Every paragraph teaches; omit routine limitations, roadmap language, and em dashes. Every content slide has original source imagery; preserve study figures and add a few credited cell, anatomy, or animal images when they clarify the concept. Match every recording and added image to the adjacent teaching, not merely its availability; textbook crops and intact primary-article panels are allowed, generated figures are never allowed. For new Chapter 2 and later decks, embed exactly 20 academic plus 20 separately credited aesthetic/visual-context recordings, totaling 40 distinct videos, each directly aligned with the concept taught on its slide, preserving native resolution, timing, sound, and proportions. Replace blocked papers with accessible suitable primary studies unless indispensable; stop final delivery for blocked selected necessary videos and request exact uploads. Verify references, crops, media bytes/relationships, source roles, count, and rendered layout. Never claim to have inspected sources that are unavailable. For Chapter 1, replace careers/study-strategy material with actual new neurotechnology, including substantial optogenetics coverage and the instructor’s requested research examples.

Apply course/TEACHING_STYLE.md throughout the slides and speaker-note transcripts. Explain the biology as a professor would: define structures and proteins, describe their actions, and explain the source-supported changes in signaling, cell shape, firing, or behavior. Every paragraph adds science, including the last paragraph. Delete generic research summaries such as "the study brings drug action back to a complete causal sequence," "this places the mechanism in a broader context," or lists saying that several factors matter. Replace them with the actual transport step, molecular action, response to an inhibitor, time-dependent change, anatomical detail, or behavioral result. Do not hide a missing explanation behind technical vocabulary. Read all prose aloud and apply the deletion test described in the style guide; passing the automated phrase checks is insufficient.

# Behavioral Neuroscience 392

Connected repository: https://github.com/jordanxxlopez/BEHAVNEUR-392-.git. The trailing hyphen is part of its name. Neuroethology source tools were copied from the current default branch at commit 5045962, then adapted here without changing NEUR 411.

See AGENTS.md and course/policy.json for course-only requirements. There will be 19 chapter decks, preferably 75 slides each, at most 85; 30–40% textbook foundations and 60–70% primary research, interwoven throughout the lecture; exactly 20 academic and 20 aesthetic embedded videos (40 total) for Chapter 2 and subsequent new decks, each aligned with its slide’s subject. Existing Chapter 1 deliveries retain their original media counts. The textbook contents and first chapter mapping have been verified. The builder retains Neuroethology content layouts and changes the title slide to white with a source image left and instructor details right.

[Teaching prose and transcript requirements](course/TEACHING_STYLE.md) apply to every chapter and authorized revision. Follow the instructor's supplied plain-language example: explain terms as they arise, describe what changes in the cell or animal, and develop connected scientific explanations. Generic study wrap-ups and unexplained strings of technical names do not satisfy the teaching requirement. Chapter 4 has been revised throughout; its slide structure, source imagery, and 40 embedded recordings are preserved.

All six split textbook parts are available in private source storage. Chapter 1 (Introduction, printed pages 15–34) and the table of contents have been reviewed; 19 chapters are confirmed. The prior professor’s three early lectures have been inspected. Three retained EVE excerpts from Neuroethology Lecture 94 have been copied unchanged for reuse. The first deck has a separate Version 2: 75 slides with 30 embedded videos (20 academic and ten visual-context), shorter concrete teaching prose, and 39.7% foundations / 60.3% research. Version 1 remains unchanged. See chapters/C01/version2/STATUS.md and VIDEO_INDEX.md. The PPTX is editable; its accompanying PDF is a static preview.

## Commands

- `python -m pip install -r requirements.txt`
- `python tools/crop_figure.py source.pdf PAGE --preview preview.png`
- `python tools/build_lecture.py chapters/C01/lecture.json`
- Embed source videos and record their provenance in `media_sources.json`.
- `python tools/check_lecture.py chapter.pptx --lecture 1 --content-slides 73`
- `python tools/check_course.py chapters/C01/lecture.json chapter.pptx media_sources.json`
- `soffice --headless --convert-to pdf chapter.pptx` for static visual QA.

The blank template intentionally cannot build a final chapter. The generic checker is necessary but insufficient: the course checker also verifies the chapter title’s verified status, total slides, teaching-source balance, imagery, distinct video quotas, and embedded hashes. Actual desktop PowerPoint playback still needs checking after final media integration.

The expanded Version 2 retains the same slide order, study figures and 30 embedded videos. Every content paragraph now has 5–7 actual rendered lines, verified individually by tools/check_paragraph_lines.py. Use chapters/C01/version2/lecture_expanded.json to rebuild this revision, then embed with `python chapters/C01/version2/embed_media.py lecture_expanded.json`. See PARAGRAPH_LINE_CHECK.md in that folder for all 219 counts.

The latest Chapter 1 history-expanded revision is in [chapters/C01/history_revision](chapters/C01/history_revision/STATUS.md): 90 slides under a lecture-specific authorization, preserving all previous content and 30 videos. It adds 15 historical and related research slides. All 264 content paragraphs pass the 5–7 rendered-line audit. See its VIDEO_INDEX.md and NOBEL_STUDY_MAP.md. Other chapters retain the 85-slide maximum.

Central auditory pathways are reserved for Part II.

# Source access status

Source selection and verification are complete. Full references and DOI links are in lecture.json and the PPTX speaker notes. # How Nerve Cells Work: slide sequence

1. How Nerve Cells Work: From Electrical Signals to Chemical Communication
2. Neurons divide communication among specialized regions
3. The cell body maintains distant neuronal compartments
4. The cytoskeleton supports branches and carries cargo
5. Dendrites provide surfaces for incoming synaptic signals
6. Actin waves accompany bursts of neurite growth
7. Microtubule growth increases within actin waves
8. Motor-driven vesicle movement differs from diffusion
9. Developing neurons redistribute transport among branches
10. Growing processes accumulate membrane cargo locally
11. Axonal cargo delivery can change synaptic performance
12. Glia perform distinct jobs around neurons
13. Microglia engulf material from damaged or dying cells
14. Cell fragments must be distinguished from intact cells
15. Phagocytic vacuoles identify a cell's recent activity
16. Microglia can engulf debris from other microglia
17. Phagocytosis changes developmental cell survival
18. Cell maintenance operates on a different timescale
19. Phagocytosis maintains the neural environment
20. Microglial surveillance changes with brain state
21. Astrocytic calcium contributes to synaptic strengthening
22. Oligodendrocytes wrap axons with myelin membrane
23. Schwann cells myelinate peripheral axonal segments
24. Early axonal wrapping is repeatedly started and lost
25. Sheath stabilization differs from sheath initiation
26. Astrocytes supply lipids used to build central myelin
27. Extracellular lipid supply can alter myelin formation
28. Glial membrane handling shapes the final sheath pattern
29. The blood–brain barrier controls the neural environment
30. Endothelial signals help maintain a tight brain barrier
31. Astrocytes can form a second protective boundary
32. Barrier changes alter later inflammatory responses
33. Membranes maintain unequal ion concentrations
34. Membrane voltage measures charge separation
35. Fluorescent calcium sensors report intracellular chemistry
36. Visual stimuli recruit calcium responses in fish neurons
37. Calcium imaging can resolve activity in awake cortex
38. Selective permeability helps establish the resting state
39. Ion pumps maintain sodium and potassium gradients
40. Electric fish express specialized sodium channels
41. Channel inactivation limits a sodium current's duration
42. Threshold initiates a regenerative action potential
43. Sodium and potassium currents restore voltage
44. Persistent sodium current supports extreme firing
45. An action potential regenerates along an axon
46. Myelin speeds current spread between exposed nodes
47. Glia organize axonal ion-channel clusters
48. Myelin construction requires several cellular steps
49. Synapses separate the sending and receiving membranes
50. Synaptic vesicles package chemical messengers
51. A vesicle protein controls how far cargo travels
52. Presynaptic calcium triggers vesicle fusion
53. Potentiation enlarges the pool of release-ready vesicles
54. Potentiated terminals contain more docked vesicles
55. Calcium channels approach vesicle-priming sites
56. Complexin regulates spontaneous and evoked release
57. Different complexin mutations separate release functions
58. Excitatory input moves a cell toward firing threshold
59. Inhibition reduces the effect of excitatory input
60. CAPS affects excitation and inhibition unequally
61. Genetic interactions change release and movement
62. Receptors convert transmitter binding into a response
63. Synaptic inputs combine across space and time
64. Several active spines can recruit dendritic spikes
65. Dendritic responses can become larger than linear sums
66. NMDA receptors contribute to active dendritic integration
67. Reuptake and enzymes terminate transmitter action
68. Astrocytes participate in cholinergic synaptic plasticity
69. Coincident glial and neuronal activity strengthens input
70. Autoreceptors regulate a neuron's own transmitter release
71. Chemical signals can act beyond one synaptic cleft
72. Presynaptic signaling can change release probability
73. Synaptic strengthening reorganizes the release site
74. Cellular transport can alter a learned motor skill
75. Key takeaways

# Chapter 2 delivery

Title: How Nerve Cells Work: From Electrical Signals to Chemical Communication.

75 slides: title, 73 content, six-point Key takeaways. There are 29 foundation slides (39.7%) and 44 research slides (60.3%), interwoven. Every content slide has source imagery; 46 carry primary-article imagery. The independent course theme is Prussian blue / fog; the native text font is Arial.

Exactly 40 distinct recordings are embedded: 20 academic and 20 aesthetic. Duplicate channel exports, alternate motion-correction footage, and a rotating reconstruction were excluded from the count. Context recordings remain labeled separately and are not treated as primary evidence. All 40 delivery files fully decode, and their hashes match the embedded bytes. Native timing and source audio status were checked. Necessary compatibility conversions preserve the scenes and native frame rates; odd dimensions receive only one-pixel edge padding. Sampled conversion SSIM is recorded in media_validation.json; this is a first-60-frame comparison, not a whole-video quality score.

All 219 teaching paragraphs have 5–7 actual rendered lines. The generic deck checker and course checker both report zero failures; the generic checker reports zero warnings. All 75 final slides were rendered and visually reviewed. Crop boxes, figure credits, full references, exact article licenses, and media provenance are retained. The primary-figure threshold in the builder/checker now reads the course policy's 60% minimum rather than an inherited hard-coded 70%. Foundation versus research teaching roles remain independent of the figure type.

The editable PPTX contains the videos. The accompanying _Static.pdf and Presenton web/PDF preview are static and use source posters. Desktop PowerPoint playback was unavailable and remains untested. Use desktop PowerPoint Slide Show to play the embedded recordings.

The final lecture.json is authoritative. teaching_content.txt mirrors the reviewed prose. Source PDFs stay in ignored private storage, and the full uploaded textbook is never published. Existing Chapter 1 decks were not rebuilt.

Rebuild from the repository root:

python3 tools/check_paragraph_lines.py chapters/C02/lecture.json chapters/C02/How_Nerve_Cells_Work_Chapter_2.pptx chapters/C02/How_Nerve_Cells_Work_Chapter_2_Static.pdf chapters/C02/paragraph_line_check.json

python3 tools/check_course.py chapters/C02/lecture.json chapters/C02/How_Nerve_Cells_Work_Chapter_2.pptx chapters/C02/media_sources.json

# Chapter 3 delivery

Mapping the Nervous System: From Brain Structures to Behavior.

75 slides: title, 73 content, and six Key takeaways. The verified scope is Carlson and Birkett (2022), Structure of the Nervous System, printed pp. 68–90. There are 29 foundation slides and 44 research slides, interwoven. Every content slide contains source imagery; 44 use primary-article panels. Arial text uses a mineral blue / paper white theme with black body text, captions, and footers.

Exactly 40 distinct biological recordings are embedded. The two internal quotas each contain 20 recordings. Media-purpose classifications appear only in internal provenance records, never in slide prose, captions, or teaching notes. Every quarter of the content sequence has ten recordings, no gap exceeds three content slides, and the final ten content slides contain five. Source article figures remain on every recording slide.

All delivery recordings fully decode. Native dimensions, source timing, frame rate, and audio status were checked. All 40 recordings retain their exact original publisher H.264 bytes; no delivery re-encoding is used. Poster frames are sampled from actual recording content. Embedded hashes, internal video/media relationships, and native timing entries are verified by embed_media.py.

Every teaching paragraph must pass the actual 5–7-rendered-line audit against the final static PDF, tied to the final spec and PPTX hashes. Generic and course checks include image coverage, teaching balance, media quotas, visible category labels, and video distribution. Source-panel crop boxes and original legends are retained. Source documents remain private and ignored; the full uploaded book is never published.

The editable PPTX is the primary deliverable. The _Static.pdf and Presenton companion use source posters and do not play video. Desktop PowerPoint playback is unavailable in the cloud and remains untested. Open the PPTX in desktop PowerPoint Slide Show and click the recordings to play them.

Rebuild from the repository root after retrieving Git LFS assets:

```bash
python3 tools/build_lecture.py chapters/C03/lecture.json
python3 chapters/C03/embed_media.py
soffice --headless --convert-to pdf --outdir chapters/C03 chapters/C03/Mapping_the_Nervous_System_Chapter_3.pptx
cp chapters/C03/Mapping_the_Nervous_System_Chapter_3.pdf chapters/C03/Mapping_the_Nervous_System_Chapter_3_Static.pdf
python3 tools/check_paragraph_lines.py chapters/C03/lecture.json chapters/C03/Mapping_the_Nervous_System_Chapter_3.pptx chapters/C03/Mapping_the_Nervous_System_Chapter_3_Static.pdf chapters/C03/paragraph_line_check.json
python3 tools/check_lecture.py chapters/C03/Mapping_the_Nervous_System_Chapter_3.pptx --lecture 3 --content-slides 73
python3 tools/check_course.py chapters/C03/lecture.json chapters/C03/Mapping_the_Nervous_System_Chapter_3.pptx chapters/C03/media_sources.json
```

Embed only into a freshly rebuilt base deck. Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 deliverables are unchanged. The new distribution and visible-label rules apply from Chapter 3 onward.

Presenton static companion PDF: https://api.presenton.ai/s/yelwXwXPn1jOTiAg2Uswi5vZ16Bsvg79. The companion and native deck use Arial; the main static PDF is the locally rendered, paragraph-audited native deck.

1. Chemical Control of Behavior: Drugs and Neural Signaling

# Sources and chapter coverage

Carlson NR, Birkett MA (2022). Physiology of Behavior, Global Edition, 13th edition. Pearson. ISBN 9781292430256. Chapter 6, Vision, printed pp. 153–190; uploaded Part 2, PDF pages 73–92, and Part 3, PDF pages 1–18. The source chapter and review pages were read locally. # From Light to Sight: How the Brain Builds the Visual World

Completed Chapter 6 for Behavioral Neuroscience 392, Fall 2026. Jordan Lopez, Ph.D., Professor of Neurobiology & Biomedical Engineering.

The verified source chapter is **Vision**, Carlson and Birkett (2022), Global Edition, 13th edition, ISBN 9781292430256, printed pp. 153–190. The instructor authorized 85–90 slides with visual illusions and a brief treatment of rewired ferrets and plasticity.

## Content and style

90 total slides: one title, 88 teaching slides, and one closing slide with six takeaways. Foundations (32) and research teaching (56) are interwoven. Every teaching slide has three explanatory paragraphs, matching speaker-note teaching text, and credited source imagery. The prose follows the instructor's Chapter 4 correction and course/TEACHING_STYLE.md: define terms, explain mechanisms and observed changes, and use the third paragraph for substantive teaching.

Coverage includes optics, phototransduction, ON/OFF signaling, retinal receptive fields, ganglion-cell imaging, synaptic timing, LGN and cortical maps, visual connectomics, orientation selectivity, spatial frequency, color and adaptation, recognition, infant development, binocular depth, motion and gaze, optogenetic restoration, and intracortical visual prostheses. Illusions include the blind spot, surrounding brightness, scintillating starburst and grids, filtered-image recognition, illusory contours, negative afterimages, face orientation, and double drift.

Four ferret slides (31–34) explain neonatal retinal rerouting through auditory thalamus, visual receptive fields, orientation modules, and behavior. Additional plasticity examples include adult primate opsin gene therapy, infant category development, and visuomotor recalibration after cataract removal. The later audition lecture should make a short callback after its normal pathway.

The 16:9 layout uses Arial, white backgrounds, black body/caption/footer text, and restrained optical-blue headings. The title retains the course's source-image-left/instructor-details-right format. No scientific image or movie was generated, redrawn, or reconstructed. Original panel crops retain the relevant axes, scale bars, and labels. See [slide sequence](SLIDE_SPINE.md), [papers](PAPERS.md), and [recordings](VIDEO_INDEX.md).

## Validation

All 264 paragraphs pass the actual-export 5–7-line audit. Generic and course-specific checks report zero failures. All 90 rendered slides, figure crops, and recording posters were visually reviewed. All 40 distinct recordings are embedded, ten in each content quarter, with no gap beyond three teaching slides and six recordings in the final ten. All source/embedded movie hashes and package relationships resolve. Every movie passes full-file decoding; eight necessary H.264 compatibility conversions preserve native dimensions, timing, and audio. Minimum first-60-frame SSIM: 0.995537.

Source access is documented honestly: open full texts were reviewed, while the two 2000 Nature ferret papers use their public abstracts and original figure panels. Their subscription full text was not accessed. The 1992 ferret paper was read in full. See source_access_review.json and the source notes. The complete uploaded book and paper source files remain private.

Desktop PowerPoint playback has not been tested in this environment. Click movie objects in PowerPoint Slide Show; PDF and browser companions use static source posters. Exact final hashes and sizes are in VALIDATION.json.

# Audition I: From Sound to Neural Signals

The Peripheral Auditory System is the instructor-authorized 80-slide companion to Chapter 7. It contains a title, 78 teaching slides, and six final takeaways. The six regeneration and translation slides occupy slides 74–79 within the 80-slide total.

Coverage follows acoustic pressure through outer- and middle-ear mechanics, cochlear motion, hair-bundle transduction, inner-hair-cell ribbon synapses, and auditory-nerve coding. Injury, existing-cell repair, animal regeneration, experimental mammalian reprogramming, and requirements for human translation are distinguished. Central auditory pathways and binaural computations are reserved for Part II. The brief efferent material concerns peripheral terminals only.

There are 31 foundation slides and 47 primary-research teaching slides, with original source imagery on every teaching slide. Forty distinct source recordings are embedded, ten in each content quarter and six in the final ten teaching slides. Full teaching transcripts, figure legends, source references, licenses, and media provenance are in the PowerPoint notes and accompanying records.

The editable PowerPoint is `From_Sound_to_Neural_Signals_Peripheral_Auditory_System_Part_I.pptx`. Its clearly labeled `_Static.pdf` companion contains source posters. Arial is used throughout. Download the PowerPoint through the GitHub media URL or use Git LFS; a raw LFS pointer is not the presentation.

Validation covers all 234 rendered paragraphs, every source-media hash, complete audiovisual decoding, all embedded media relationships and timing, and both repository validators. See VALIDATION.json and paragraph_line_check.json. All slide layouts and selected source panels were visually reviewed. Actual desktop PowerPoint playback remains untested.

Rebuild with `assemble_spec.py`, the repository `tools/build_lecture.py`, then `embed_media.py`. Use `make_static_pdf.py` to render a temporary copy without movie objects, retaining posters; exporting the multimedia deck directly can place large media objects into the PDF. Rerun `tools/check_paragraph_lines.py`, `tools/check_lecture.py --lecture 71 --content-slides 78`, and `tools/check_course.py` after a change. Keep all full textbook and article downloads private and ignored.

The Presenton static companion and shareable preview are recorded in presenton_preview.json. Presenton links expire after 24 hours; the repository download links remain available.

----- END ORIGINAL SOURCE -----

# Sensing the Body and the Chemical World

**Balance, Touch, Pain, Taste, and Smell** — Chapter 7, Behavioral Neuroscience 392.

This is the instructor-authorized **nonauditory** Chapter 7 lecture. Audition and hearing are excluded and reserved for a separate future lecture. The supplied Carlson and Birkett (2022), *Physiology of Behavior*, Global Edition, 13th edition, ISBN 9781292430256, was inspected directly: Chapter 7 is printed pp. 191–234. This deck covers the vestibular, somatosensory, gustatory, and olfactory material on printed pp. **210–234**, Part 3 PDF pp. **38–62**. Chapter 8 starts printed p. 235.

## Downloads

- [Editable PowerPoint, including 40 embedded recordings](https://media.githubusercontent.com/media/jordanxxlopez/BEHAVNEUR-392-/main/chapters/C07/Sensing_the_Body_and_the_Chemical_World_Chapter_7.pptx), approximately 255 MB.
- [Static PDF preview](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jordanxxlopez/BEHAVNEUR-392-/main/chapters/C07/Sensing_the_Body_and_the_Chemical_World_Chapter_7_Static.pdf), approximately 11 MB. Uses source posters; contains no playable video objects.

## Teaching sequence

75 slides: title, 73 teaching slides, and six exam-level takeaways on the closing slide.

| Slides | Coverage |
|---|---|
| 2–9 | Vestibular sensation, hair bundles, canals, otolith organs, gaze stabilization, and coordination |
| 10–28 | Skin receptors, touch, sensory pathways, proprioception, and cortical representations |
| 29–33 | Temperature, itch, scratching, and chemical irritation |
| 34–50 | Nociception, pain, spinal processing, descending modulation, opioids, and attention |
| 51–61 | Taste cells, transduction, pathways, feeding decisions, and flavor |
| 62–74 | Olfactory receptors, glomeruli, circuit development, learning, and odor-guided navigation |

29 foundation slides (39.7%) and 44 research slides (60.3%) are interwoven. The scope retains a brief sensory explanation of muscle spindles without moving the detailed Chapter 8 motor-control material into this deck. Human studies include somatosensory-cortex stimulation, attentional analgesia, and odor-mixture learning. Mammalian and fly receptor mechanisms are distinguished, as are pain and nociception, calcium fluorescence and electrical recordings, and taste and flavor. Five familiar taste qualities and research on oral fatty-acid sensing are distinguished rather than presenting all nutrient preferences as equally established human taste categories.

The 16:9 editable deck uses Arial, a white title slide with the source image left and instructor information right, black body text, and a sapphire/silver theme. Every teaching slide has three substantive paragraphs and a matching teaching transcript before the references in notes. All content slides retain original source imagery; 44 use primary-article figures. Figures are never redrawn or recolored. Original source-panel crops and full legends are recorded in figure_sources.json. Textbook coordinates distinguish the visible CropBox from the MediaBox used by the crop tool.

Exactly 40 distinct original publisher MP4s are embedded: 20 academic and 20 visual-context recordings. All 40 movies retain their original bytes, resolution, timing, frame rate, and audio presence; no delivery conversion was necessary. Full FFmpeg decoding passes for all recordings. Embedded hashes, internal video and media relationships, and native PowerPoint timing entries are verified. Source posters are sampled from actual recording content.

All 219 paragraphs pass the 5–7 actual rendered-line requirement using Arial, with no forced line breaks or blank-line padding. The audit identifies the exact final specification, PPTX, and static PDF by SHA256. Generic and course checks report zero failures; the generic checker reports zero warnings. All slides and source-panel sheets were visually reviewed. VALIDATION.json, paragraph_line_check.json, media_validation.json, PAPERS.md, VIDEO_INDEX.md, and SLIDE_SPINE.md retain the evidence.

**Desktop PowerPoint playback remains untested.** Open the PPTX in desktop PowerPoint Slide Show and click movie objects. The PDF and Presenton companion are static. Full textbook PDFs and downloaded article sources remain private and ignored.

## Rebuild

The final **lecture.json is authoritative**. Assembly scripts record initial preparation and must not overwrite later reviewed changes blindly. Retrieve Git LFS assets first. Embed only into a freshly rebuilt base deck.

```bash
cd /workspace/BEHAVNEUR-392-
source /workspace/.venvs/behavneur/bin/activate
export PATH=/workspace/.setup/bin:$PATH
export FONTCONFIG_FILE=/workspace/.setup/fonts.conf
python tools/build_lecture.py chapters/C07/lecture.json
python chapters/C07/embed_media.py
python chapters/C07/make_static_pdf.py
python tools/check_paragraph_lines.py chapters/C07/lecture.json chapters/C07/Sensing_the_Body_and_the_Chemical_World_Chapter_7.pptx chapters/C07/Sensing_the_Body_and_the_Chemical_World_Chapter_7_Static.pdf chapters/C07/paragraph_line_check.json
python tools/check_lecture.py chapters/C07/Sensing_the_Body_and_the_Chemical_World_Chapter_7.pptx --lecture 7 --content-slides 73
python tools/check_course.py chapters/C07/lecture.json chapters/C07/Sensing_the_Body_and_the_Chemical_World_Chapter_7.pptx chapters/C07/media_sources.json
python chapters/C07/validate_recordings.py
```

The static renderer uses an ignored temporary PowerPoint copy with movie objects removed and original poster shapes retained. This avoids embedding multimedia in the static PDF while preserving native text and layout. It leaves the primary editable PPTX unchanged. On other machines, install the Python requirements plus PyMuPDF, use a compatible LibreOffice installation, and make licensed Arial available before claiming final line-count compliance.

A Presenton static companion is recorded in presenton_preview.json. Its HTML uses the exact final static pages and source credits; full source PDFs were not uploaded. The HTML declares Arial, matching the rendered native text. Presenton download and browser-preview links expire after 24 hours; repository downloads remain the primary deliverables.

## Content

100 slides: title, 98 teaching slides, and six exam-level takeaways. There are 32 foundation slides and 66 primary-research teaching slides, with original article figures on 84 slides. Every teaching slide has three connected explanatory paragraphs and matching speaker-note teaching text. All 294 paragraphs pass the actual-render five-to-seven-line audit. Source credits, full references, and original figure/movie legends accompany the teaching notes.

Coverage includes central brainstem timing, myelin and inhibition, population coding, inferior colliculus, auditory thalamus, core/belt/parabelt cortex, descending feedback, auditory scenes and attention, multisensory speech and illusions, learned predictions, voice and timbre, pitch, musical expectation, beat and movement, comparative rhythm, improvisation, white matter, developmental music experience, cognitive control, music-evoked nostalgia, auditory learning windows, vocal communication, active echolocation, selective recognition deficits, a brief rewired-ferret callback, and reconstruction of heard music from cortical recordings. Four accessible USC Brain and Creativity Institute studies receive explicit coverage. The chapter supplies the central auditory foundation; peripheral anatomy, mechanics, and hair-cell transduction remain in the separate Audition I deck.

## Format and validation

16:9, Arial throughout, white backgrounds, black body/captions/footers, rosewood headings. The title retains the source-image-left/instructor-details-right format. All scientific figures and movies are original source material; no scientific image was generated or redrawn. Source-derived simulations and anatomical reconstructions are identified. Crops were made with tools/crop_figure.py and recorded with original hashes and boxes.

All 100 slides were rendered and reviewed. Generic and course-specific checks report zero failures. Fifty distinct videos are embedded, distributed 13/12/13/12 by content quarter, with five in the final ten teaching slides and no gap exceeding one slide. Every movie passes full-file decoding. All source and embedded hashes match; all package relationships and native media timing entries resolve. Compatibility conversions preserve timing and dimensions, apart from one documented one-pixel edge pad; the minimum first-60-frame SSIM is 0.987010. The static PDF contains 100 pages and no video attachments. The Presenton PDF is a separate static companion; fonts: Arial, system font, no web-font source.

**Desktop PowerPoint playback has not been tested in this environment.** Click a recording in PowerPoint Slide Show. The PDFs and browser companion display static posters.

Read [slide sequence](SLIDE_SPINE.md), [sources](PAPERS.md), [recording index](VIDEO_INDEX.md), and [validation](VALIDATION.json). The original nonauditory Chapter 7 and the separate peripheral lecture are preserved. The complete uploaded book and full papers remain private and ignored. Subscription access to the 2000 ferret paper was not obtained; its abstract and original figure are distinguished from the fully read 1992 anatomy paper.

# Embedded recordings

50 distinct source recordings, distributed 13/12/13/12 across the four consecutive quarters of the 98 teaching slides. No gap exceeds one content slide; five recordings occur in the final ten. Internal purpose classifications are retained only in the machine-readable manifest, outside visible slide text and teaching notes.

Original recordings include real animal behavior, original experimental stimuli, tissue-derived anatomical reconstructions, and source-authored analytical simulations. Each is identified accurately in the teaching text and source legend. An anatomical rotation does not represent live neural firing. The three cortical electrode-placement movies accompany different participants; the two mouse approach movies are separate intact-song trials rather than opposite experimental conditions. Audio-only supplements were excluded from the 50-video count.

Source dimensions, frame rates, timing, and supplied soundtracks are preserved. Eight files require H.264 compatibility conversion; seven require lossless container remuxing. One odd-sized source receives a one-pixel edge pad. Two PCM soundtracks require AAC encoding at the original sample rate and channel count. Source originals remain available for byte/hash verification. Desktop PowerPoint playback is untested; static PDF and browser previews display source posters.

# From Intention to Action: The Neural Control of Movement

75 slides.

1. Title
2. Movement requires force, coordination, and a goal
3. Muscles pull across joints to produce movement

9. A muscle action potential releases stored calcium

36. Motor and sensory cortex share detail but differ in timing

69. Constructional difficulty concerns spatial organization
70. Developmental coordination difficulties need assessment
71. Finger representations can persist after paralysis

73. Cerebellar disorders have different neural spike signatures
74. Imposing abnormal spike patterns can alter movement

# From Intention to Action: The Neural Control of Movement

Chapter 8 contains 75 slides: title, 73 teaching slides, and six final takeaways on the last slide. Coverage follows muscle physiology and the neuromuscular junction through proprioception, spinal reflexes, locomotor circuits, descending pathways, motor planning, basal ganglia, cerebellum, reaching and grasping, apraxia, and movement disorders. A brain–computer interface example distinguishes decoded virtual finger control from physical recovery.

The lecture contains 29 foundation and 44 primary-research slides, with original source imagery on every teaching slide. Forty distinct original MP4 recordings are embedded with source posters, ten per content quarter and six in the final ten teaching slides. Teaching transcripts match all three substantive paragraphs per teaching slide; notes include figure legends, full references, source-recording identities, credits, licenses, and relevant preparation distinctions.

The editable PowerPoint is `From_Intention_to_Action_Control_of_Movement_Chapter_8.pptx`. Its `_Static.pdf` companion contains source posters. Arial is used throughout. The GitHub media download serves the actual PowerPoint; a raw Git LFS pointer is not the deck.

Validation records are saved separately in VALIDATION.json, paragraph_line_check.json, and media_validation.json. Desktop PowerPoint playback has not been tested.

Rebuild with `assemble_spec.py`, repository `tools/build_lecture.py`, and `embed_media.py`; render with `make_static_pdf.py`. Recheck actual PDF paragraph lines and both repository validators after any change. Full textbooks and article downloads must remain private. Presenton provides a separate static PDF companion and shareable preview, whose links expire after 24 hours.

Chapter 10 contains 80 slides: title, 78 teaching slides, and six exam-level takeaways on the last slide. Coverage includes reproductive differentiation, endocrine feedback and cycles, mating circuits, human sex traits and orientation, pair bonding, parental motivation, infant cues, oxytocin-dependent learning, paternal and alloparental care.

# Feeling and Acting: The Neural Systems of Emotion

Chapter 11 contains 80 slides: title, 78 teaching slides, and six exam-level takeaways on the last slide. Coverage includes components of emotion, threat learning and action selection, extinction and counterconditioning, aggression, hormonal and prefrontal regulation, facial and vocal communication, bodily feedback, interoception, empathy, and helping.

There are 31 foundation slides and 47 research slides, with original source imagery on every teaching slide. Forty distinct original recordings are embedded, internally 20 academic and 20 aesthetic, ten per teaching quarter and six in the final ten teaching slides. All 234 substantive paragraphs have matching teaching transcripts in notes. Notes also contain full references, original figure legends, recording identities, source credits, licenses, and preparation distinctions.

The editable PowerPoint is `Feeling_and_Acting_Emotion_Chapter_11.pptx`. The `_Static.pdf` companion retains original recording posters. Arial is used throughout. The GitHub media download serves the actual PowerPoint rather than a Git LFS pointer.

Validation records: VALIDATION.json, paragraph_line_check.json, media_validation.json. Every slide and source panel was visually reviewed. All original recordings were fully decoded with FFmpeg. Native PowerPoint movie relationships, timing, and embedded hashes were checked. Desktop PowerPoint playback has not been tested.

Rebuild with write_content.py, assemble_spec.py, repository tools/build_lecture.py, and embed_media.py; render with make_static_pdf.py. Run the actual PDF paragraph-line audit and both repository validators after any changes. Presenton supplies a static PDF companion and preview; these API links expire after 24 hours. Full source books and articles remain private.

# Hunger, Thirst, and Satiety: How the Brain Controls Ingestion

Chapter 12 contains 80 slides: title, 78 teaching slides, and six exam-level takeaways on the last slide. Coverage includes osmotic and volumetric thirst, anticipatory oral and gastrointestinal feedback, vasopressin, fuel storage and metabolism, AgRP and POMC circuits, gut hormones and visceral afferents, food reward, obesity, GLP-1 therapies, bariatric surgery, and eating disorders.

There are 31 foundation and 47 research slides, with original source imagery on every teaching slide. Forty distinct original recordings are embedded, ten per teaching quarter and six in the final ten teaching slides. All 234 substantive paragraphs have matching teaching transcripts in notes. Notes contain full references, available publisher legends, source identities, credits, license statements, and preparation distinctions.

Editable PowerPoint: `Hunger_Thirst_and_Satiety_Ingestive_Behavior_Chapter_12.pptx`. The `_Static.pdf` companion retains source posters. Arial is used throughout. GitHub media download URLs serve the actual deck rather than Git LFS pointer text.

Checks are recorded in VALIDATION.json, paragraph_line_check.json, and media_validation.json. Slides and source panels were visually reviewed; all recordings were fully decoded with FFmpeg. Embedded hashes, movie relationships, native source bytes, and timing were checked. Desktop PowerPoint playback has not been tested.

Rebuild with write_content.py, assemble_spec.py, tools/build_lecture.py, and embed_media.py; render with make_static_pdf.py. Re-run the actual PDF paragraph-line audit and both repository validators after changes. Presenton supplies a separate static PDF companion and shareable preview; API links expire after 24 hours. Full source books and articles remain private.

Cross-course source check: all 141 source catalogs on the current Neuroethology default branch were retrieved at fa278dba43f4bb18527b3237845da0189a37ec24. No selected DOI overlap was found; see cross_course_source_check.json.

# From Experience to Memory: Learning, Plasticity, and Recall

Chapter 13 contains 80 slides: title, 78 teaching slides, and six exam-level takeaways on the last slide. Coverage includes conditioning, reinforcement and credit assignment, habits and skills, perceptual and working memory, relational and spatial memory, hippocampal ensembles, consolidation and replay, amnesia, retrieval and forgetting, NMDA-dependent calcium entry, AMPA trafficking, spine plasticity, protein synthesis, and compensating maintenance mechanisms.

There are 31 foundation and 47 research slides, with original source imagery on every teaching slide. Forty distinct original recordings are embedded, ten per teaching quarter and six in the final ten teaching slides. All 234 substantive paragraphs have matching teaching transcripts in notes. Notes contain full references, available publisher legends, source identities, credits, license statements, and preparation distinctions.

Editable PowerPoint: `From_Experience_to_Memory_Learning_and_Memory_Chapter_13.pptx`. The `_Static.pdf` companion retains source posters. Arial is used throughout. GitHub media download URLs serve the actual deck rather than Git LFS pointer text.

Checks are recorded in VALIDATION.json, paragraph_line_check.json, and media_validation.json. Slides and source panels were visually reviewed; all recordings were fully decoded with FFmpeg. Embedded hashes, movie relationships, native source bytes, and timing were checked. Desktop PowerPoint playback has not been tested.

Rebuild with write_content.py, assemble_spec.py, tools/build_lecture.py, and embed_media.py; render with make_static_pdf.py. Re-run the actual PDF paragraph-line audit and both repository validators after changes. Presenton supplies a separate static PDF companion and shareable preview; API links expire after 24 hours. Full source books and articles remain private.

Cross-course source check: all 141 source catalogs on the current Neuroethology default branch were retrieved at fa278dba43f4bb18527b3237845da0189a37ec24. No selected DOI overlap was found; see cross_course_source_check.json.

# Recording alignment revision

The 80-slide lecture retains 40 distinct embedded recordings: **26 newly sourced recordings and 14 retained recordings**, assigned to their directly matching material. Twenty are classified as academic and twenty as observational in the internal manifest. Only one USC vocal-tract MRI remains, on articulatory movement (slide 10).

Slide 46 now uses a real patient reading examination during occipitotemporal electrical stimulation. Other additions include nonfluent and fluent aphasia examinations, poststroke language testing, signed-language stimuli, word-selective cortical localization, diffusion tractography, and clinical speech-decoding demonstrations. Each caption names what is shown; notes explain what students should observe.

Recordings follow concepts rather than a uniform interval: quarters contain 12/7/7/14 recordings; the single four-slide video-free interval covers slides 42–45. All original teaching paragraphs, titles, figures, and the 80-slide sequence are preserved.

| Slide | Recording | What to observe |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | Larsen & Stensaas: naming, repetition, reading and writing. | Watch the examiner separate spontaneous speech, object naming, sentence repetition, reading and writing. These are observable components of human communication in the opening slide. |
| 3 | Dieguez-Campa et al. (2026): aphasia after a right-hemisphere stroke. | This published case shows the patient’s language impairment after a right-hemisphere stroke. Relate the clinical behavior to the case’s atypical lateralization, established by the lesion history; the movie is a clinical examination, not a functional activation scan. |
| 6 | Larsen & Stensaas: category-word generation. | Watch the participant generate category members. Word retrieval also requires maintaining the task rule and continuing the search, matching the overlap between language and frontal control on this slide. |
| 7 | Nakai et al. (2017): cortical activity during auditory naming. | Watch the real patient-derived cortical activity maps evolve from hearing a description to preparing and producing a name. The high-gamma and beta panels show distinct physiological changes across the language network. |
| 8 | Livingstone & Russo (2018): audiovisual speech. | Watch the visible lip and jaw movements while hearing the same utterance. The face supplies visual speech information that can be compared with the acoustic syllables. |
| 10 | USC SPAN / Esling (2015): lips close and release for /p/. | Watch complete lip closure and the release of the voiceless bilabial plosive. This is a directly visible articulatory mechanism, placed only on the speech-movement slide. |
| 12 | Stavisky et al. (2019): spoken syllables and motor-cortex spikes. | Listen to each prompted syllable and compare it with the simultaneously recorded electrode activity. This is the same study as the slide’s neural-pattern figure. |
| 14 | Woolnough et al. (2019): cortical activity around articulation. | Watch the original time-resolved activity maps before and after articulation. Interpret posterior-insula recruitment with the timing and coverage described in the slide and original source legend. |
| 15 | Stavisky et al. (2019): neural trajectories aligned to speech onset. | Watch the original population trajectories evolve relative to acoustic onset. Their progression directly illustrates the slide’s distinction between neural activity before and after spoken output. |
| 16 | Metzger et al. (2023): attempted words versus finger movements. | Watch the same cortical interface distinguish attempted NATO code words from attempted finger flexions. This provides a second, clearly identified example of different operations being distinguishable within a shared recorded cortical system. |
| 19 | Larsen & Stensaas: similarities and proverb meanings. | Listen to explanations of similarities and proverbs. Correctly pronouncing a phrase and explaining its conceptual meaning require different operations, as the slide explains. |
| 20 | Larsen & Stensaas: following spoken and written commands. | Watch the participant translate verbal instructions into the requested actions. Tracking which action applies to which object makes sentence relationships clinically observable. |
| 24 | Livingstone & Russo (2018): happy delivery of the same sentence. | Compare this happy delivery with the angry recording beside it. The words and speaker are held constant while pitch, rhythm and affective delivery change. |
| 24 | Livingstone & Russo (2018): angry delivery of the same sentence. | Compare this angry delivery with the happy recording beside it. Listen for prosodic changes rather than a change in the sentence’s lexical content. |
| 27 | Livingstone & Russo (2018): a different speaker, the same words. | Compare this female actor’s voice with the male actor in the prosody examples. The same sentence can retain its linguistic content while speaker identity changes. |
| 30 | Feng et al. (2025): poststroke language tests, SLT-only patients. | Watch actual poststroke speech-language testing before and after intensive speech-language therapy in the source’s SLT-only group. Naming and connected speech are observable clinical outcomes. |
| 33 | Larsen & Stensaas: nonfluent expressive aphasia. | Watch effortful, short speech output, sentence repetition and writing during the examination of a patient with expressive aphasia. Compare preserved understanding with impaired sentence production. |
| 36 | Larsen & Stensaas: fluent receptive aphasia (audio). | Listen to fluent output with naming difficulty and words or phrases that do not communicate the intended meaning. The original source is an audio-only clinical recording with a static audio symbol; listen rather than treating the symbol as brain imaging. |
| 40 | Bogliotti & Isel (2021): manual signs and mouthing in French Sign Language. | Watch the original five manual/mouthing conditions and their displayed condition labels. Manual signs and mouth actions provide visual linguistic information; compare lexical and incongruent combinations. |
| 41 | Twomey et al. (2020): British Sign Language sentence stimulus. | Watch a natural-language sentence conveyed visually in British Sign Language. It demonstrates what accessible signed linguistic input looks like. The recording is a stimulus from the cited early-exposure study, not a recording of language deprivation or a diagnosis. |
| 46 | Marchive et al. (2025): word reading during cortical stimulation. | Watch the patient read before, during and after left occipitotemporal stimulation, including the difficulty signal. This directly demonstrates selective disruption of visual word access. |
| 48 | Nordt et al. (2023): developing visual-category representations. | Watch the original category-representation spaces for left and right ventral temporal cortex change between age groups. Light-blue circles are words. This is a published interpolation of measured age-group representations, not continuous imaging of one growing brain. |
| 52 | Marchive et al. (2025): letter-by-letter reading with word-reading failure. | Watch the patient identify letters while struggling to assemble the written word. This is the reading-route dissociation described on the acquired-dyslexia slide. |
| 55 | Mitchell et al. (2025): locating the visual word-form area. | Watch the authors identify a word-selective cortical region on an individual reconstructed brain surface. The video shows anatomical localization of the VWFA used in their dyslexia study; color marks the functional contrast, not a diagnostic scan for an individual child. |
| 56 | Wang et al. (2023): diffusion-based language-pathway reconstruction. | Watch a three-dimensional reconstruction of the language pathways derived from diffusion imaging. These are estimated fiber bundles from the source template, illustrating what a tractography reconstruction represents; the animation does not itself display the adjacent reading-skill correlation. |
| 58 | Marchive et al. (2025): rapid letter naming during cortical stimulation. | Watch rapid letter naming deteriorate during stimulation. Efficient visual recognition depends on processing speed as well as eventual letter identification, making this a clinical counterexample to fluent visual word expertise. |
| 61 | Willett et al. (2021): handwriting versus cursor typing. | Watch the same participant communicate through two different motor organizations: attempted handwriting and point-and-click cursor typing. The original side-by-side demonstration illustrates different ways to organize a written message. |
| 62 | Willett et al. (2021): hand micromovements during attempted writing. | Watch the patient’s hand during attempted handwriting. The tiny residual movements distinguish attempted writing from restored useful hand function. |
| 63 | Willett et al. (2021): handwriting-decoded text in real time. | Watch sentence text emerge from the handwriting brain-computer interface as the participant attempts each character. This is the decoder output corresponding to the character-based approach described on the slide. |
| 65 | Pandarinath et al. (2017): a patient types spontaneous answers. | Watch participant T6 formulate an answer and use a brain-controlled cursor to select letters. This is the exact cortical-cursor communication study taught on the slide. |
| 66 | Pandarinath et al. (2017): selecting letters on a QWERTY interface. | Watch cursor trajectories and letter selection with the QWERTY layout. Compare its arrangement with the OPTI-II keyboard in the preceding slide and the source figure. |
| 68 | Willett et al. (2023): attempted speech decoded in real time. | Watch a participant with ALS attempt sentences while a cortical decoder produces text and synthesized speech. Her impaired acoustic output and preserved intended sentence are separately observable. |
| 69 | Metzger et al. (2023): phonetic decoding of new sentences. | Watch a phoneme-based decoder convert silently attempted, previously untrained sentences into text. The original three-dot speech-detection indicator precedes the final text. This is a separately credited clinical example of the phonetic-to-sentence pipeline. |
| 70 | Metzger et al. (2023): communication after brainstem-stroke paralysis. | Watch text, synthesized voice and a facial avatar generated from the participant’s silently attempted sentences. The source patient’s speech paralysis follows brainstem stroke; the interface accesses intended language through preserved cortical signals. |
| 71 | Metzger et al. (2023): classifying attempted mouth movements. | Watch the interface distinguish six attempted nonspeech orofacial actions and animate the corresponding avatar movement. These are articulatory actions, illustrating motor representations underlying speech; they are not decoded emotions or unrestricted thoughts. |
| 72 | Anumanchipalli et al. (2019): decoded articulation and synthesized speech. | Watch the original decoded vocal-tract movements, reconstructed spectrogram and synthesized audio, followed by the recorded sentence. This is the same movement-based synthesis study as the slide. |
| 73 | Metzger et al. (2023): personalized voice and avatar, offline. | Listen to speech reconstructed from neural recordings and converted to the participant’s personalized voice using a short pre-injury voice sample. The original video is an offline voice-conversion demonstration, clearly distinct from a live conversation. |
| 75 | Willett et al. (2023): silent mouthing decoded into sentences. | Watch the cued silent-speaking condition. The participant silently mouths prompted words; this directly illustrates why the demonstration does not establish unrestricted inner-speech reading. |
| 77 | Pandarinath et al. (2017): cortical cursor with dwell selection. | Watch participant T7 select letters by dwelling on targets using the cortical interface. The source participant has paralysis; successful letter selection does not require normal overt hand movement. |
| 79 | Willett et al. (2021): freely answering questions through attempted writing. | Watch the participant formulate a novel answer and communicate it through attempted handwriting. The final example combines preserved language, spelling, motor representation and an external output route. |

Every source was checked against its original preparation. Some recordings illustrate a mechanism rather than reproduce the adjacent study; the source reference makes that distinction explicit. Original scientific images and recordings were not generated. Three unusually large clinical recordings were compressed at native resolution and timing; whole-movie SSIM exceeds 0.994 and the original audio packets are identical. The remaining 37 movies retain original published bytes. Full-source books and articles remain private.

Desktop PowerPoint playback remains untested.

# From Words to Meaning: The Neural Systems of Human Communication

Chapter 14 contains 80 slides: title, 78 teaching slides, and six exam-level takeaways on the last slide. Coverage includes language lateralization, speech production and perception, semantics and syntax, prosody, aphasia, signed language, stuttering, reading and writing, and communication neuroprostheses.

There are 31 foundation and 47 research slides, with original source imagery on every teaching slide. Forty distinct source recordings are embedded, placed beside their matching concepts. All 234 substantive paragraphs have matching teaching transcripts in notes. Notes contain full references, available publisher legends, source identities, credits, license statements, and preparation distinctions.

Editable PowerPoint: `From_Words_to_Meaning_Human_Communication_Chapter_14.pptx`. The `_Static.pdf` companion retains source posters. Arial is used throughout. GitHub media download URLs serve the actual deck rather than Git LFS pointer text.

Checks are recorded in VALIDATION.json, paragraph_line_check.json, and media_validation.json. Slides and source panels were visually reviewed; all recordings were fully decoded with FFmpeg. Embedded hashes, movie relationships, native source bytes, and timing were checked. Desktop PowerPoint playback has not been tested.

Rebuild with write_content.py, assemble_spec.py, tools/build_lecture.py, and embed_media.py; render with make_static_pdf.py. Re-run the actual PDF paragraph-line audit and both repository validators after changes. The revised static PDF companion contains the corrected source posters. Prior Presenton exports predate this media correction and should not be used. Full source books and articles remain private.

Cross-course check: all 141 current Neuroethology catalogs at fa278dba43f4bb18527b3237845da0189a37ec24 were read. No selected DOI overlaps were found; see cross_course_source_check.json.

## Media correction, 2026-10-22

The instructor identified unrelated articulation footage on the pure-alexia slide. The media audit replaced 26 recordings and retained or reassigned 14. Only one USC vocal-tract recording remains, on slide 10 (articulatory movement). Slide 46 now contains a patient’s stimulation-induced reading impairment. Full before/after assignments and what students should observe are in media_alignment_audit.json and MEDIA_ALIGNMENT_REVISION.md. Distribution is 12/7/7/14 by quarter, with a single four-slide gap through abstract concepts and stuttering genetics; this content-driven placement is recorded in the chapter-specific policy. Thirty-seven original MP4s retain published bytes; three clinical movies use verified native-resolution compression with copied audio. All 80 slides, teaching prose, figures, and matching teaching transcripts are retained.

All 40 native movies are configured for full-screen playback, using the standard PowerPoint `fullScrn` attribute, so original task labels and subtitles can be read during presentation. This setting has been structurally verified; desktop PowerPoint playback remains untested.

Coverage includes neurulation, progenitor division, migration, axon guidance, synapse formation, glial refinement, critical periods, neurogenesis, prenatal exposures, metabolic disorders, Down syndrome, autism, ADHD, and developing attention.

Forty distinct original recordings are embedded, ten per teaching quarter and six in the final ten teaching slides. All 234 substantive paragraphs have matching teaching transcripts in notes. Editable PowerPoint: `Building_the_Brain_Developing_Nervous_System_Chapter_15.pptx`. The `_Static.pdf` companion retains source posters. Arial is used throughout. GitHub media download URLs serve the actual deck rather than Git LFS pointer text.

Embedded hashes, movie relationships, native source bytes, and timing were checked. Desktop PowerPoint playback has not been tested.

# Source and teaching review

Scope: Carlson and Birkett (2022), Chapter 18, printed pages 580–603, uploaded Part6of6 PDF pages 60–83. The chapter includes stress physiology, prolonged and developmental exposure, immune regulation, PTSD, anxiety disorders, OCD, and treatments.

The teaching sequence interweaves 31 foundation slides with 47 research slides. Primary-source metadata, relevant results, figure legends, and recording preparations were checked against original eLife version-of-record data and accessible publisher/JATS full text. The core studies are listed in PAPERS.md.

Specific distinctions retained:

- CRH-cell activation, endocrine output, and context-dependent behavior are different measurements.
- Spinal norepinephrine effects depend on projection, cellular target, and pain preparation.
- Inflammatory neutrophil imaging is explicitly identified as a cellular preparation, not a psychological-stress experiment.
- VR context recall, danger-cue ethograms, extinction, and avoidance tasks show distinct defensive actions.
- The indirect-pathway imaging result differs from the simple prediction that direct-pathway hyperactivity explains all compulsive grooming.
- The four striatal calcium movies are baseline imaging preparations. They are not labeled as footage of fluoxetine treatment or optical inhibition.
- Human app training distinguishes subjective habit reports, objective automaticity, and later effort-based preferences.

Legacy claims are not copied uncritically: B cells produce antibodies; SSRIs inhibit reuptake rather than directly activating serotonin receptors; basal-ganglia projection neurons release inhibitory transmitter; a mouse grooming measure does not establish human obsessions. Clinical outcomes remain separate from animal and cell measurements.

Original scientific figures and publisher recordings are preserved. Textbook crops retain original labels and have exact MediaBox crop coordinates. A few figures from other assigned book chapters provide directly matching anatomy; their actual figure numbers and pages remain credited. No fabricated or redrawn scientific imagery is used.

Forty-seven cached Neuroethology catalogs were checked for selected DOI overlap; none was found. Two grooming examples from the same classifier paper serve distinct purposes: defining ordinary grooming and evaluating recognition across visual backgrounds. They are not presented as different studies or as coat-color effects on OCD.
