# Source and teaching review

Scope: Carlson and Birkett (2022), Chapter 19, printed pages 604–635, uploaded Part6of6 PDF pages 84–115. The sequence covers reinforcement, cues and relapse, vulnerability, opioids, stimulants, nicotine, alcohol, cannabis, and treatments.

There are 31 foundation slides and 47 research slides. Primary-source metadata, relevant results, original figure legends, and movie preparations were checked against eLife version-of-record data and accessible publisher/JATS full text. PAPERS.md records the primary sources.

Specific distinctions retained:

- Positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, punishment, tolerance, physical dependence, and substance use disorder have separate definitions.
- The odor-learning dopamine projection terminates in medial olfactory tubercle, not nucleus accumbens.
- Visual dopamine responses, psychomotor sensitization, incentive-related anticipatory behavior, and subjective pleasure are not treated as one measurement.
- Mu- and delta-receptor trafficking experiments use their actual receptors and preparations. Golgi delta-receptor signaling is not presented as footage of maintenance treatment.
- The first receptor-labeling depth series uses an FMOR mouse with a tagged receptor. The later rat preparation demonstrates native receptors without requiring a genetically tagged receptor.
- The cocaine calcium movies are a baseline and the same field after acute application. Drug seeking was measured separately in animals.
- The fluorescent drug sensor and its structural movie are not nicotinic receptor channels. ER and plasma-membrane fluorescence measure compartmental access, not clinical efficacy.
- Worm nicotine and ethanol experiments are explicit sensory-motor or channel assays, not complete human addiction models.
- CB1 locomotor movies are not mislabeled as eyelid-conditioning sessions. Global receptor deletion can alter the state in which learning is tested.

Legacy treatment claims are corrected: buprenorphine/naloxone is not described as having zero misuse potential; naloxone rescue differs from maintenance; acamprosate's complete therapeutic mechanism remains under study; CBD is not a guaranteed antipsychotic treatment or simply a universal CB1 antagonist. Clinical diagnosis and treatment language remains non-stigmatizing while the assigned chapter title is preserved.

Original scientific imagery is retained, including the publisher's own sensor and molecular visualizations. The CB1 somatodendritic recording is an explicitly identified callback to a previously taught cellular mechanism. The worm receptor study also serves a new receptor-specific teaching purpose. Forty-seven cached Neuroethology source catalogs showed no selected DOI overlap. No repeated excerpt is counted as a separate recording.

# CTE lecture sources and validation

This is an instructor-authorized special-topic lecture, not Chapter 20. The editable native deliverable is in `downloads/Brain_Injury_in_Football_CTE.pptx`; the static PDF is alongside it. Scientific references and source figure legends are in lecture.json, sources.json, and figure_sources.json. Player image credits are in player_images.json. Source movie URLs, licenses, hashes, dimensions, full timing, audio, and compatibility conversion details are in media_sources.json.

Original large source recordings and private uploaded textbooks are not duplicated in this branch. The 40 final MP4s are already embedded inside the PPTX. Rebuilding requires obtaining each original recording from the exact manifest URL and verifying its recorded hash, then applying only the documented compatibility conversion where required.

The course builder creates the base editable deck. The CTE media script embeds the originals, finalization adds source links, and the static render script retains original posters. Final rendered line checks, course checks, and media audits are recorded in VALIDATION.json and the associated JSON reports. All 80 slides use Arial. Desktop PowerPoint playback remains untested.

# Recording index

The source-specific captions and observations below correspond to embedded movies in the native PowerPoint.

## Slide 2: Michigan–Northwestern football plays. FOX Sports (2018).

The defining lesion contains abnormal phosphorylated tau in neurons around small vessels, especially at the depths of cortical folds. A lesion is a localized area of pathological change. Its cellular and anatomical arrangement distinguishes CTE from simply detecting some tau in an older person's brain.

 FOX Sports  (2018). Northwestern vs. Michigan FOX-COLLEGE-FOOTBALL-HIGHLIGHTS.webm. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Northwestern_vs._Michigan_FOX-COLLEGE-FOOTBALL-HIGHLIGHTS.webm

Original: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0b/Northwestern_vs._Michigan_FOX-COLLEGE-FOOTBALL-HIGHLIGHTS.webm

## Slide 4: Calculated stress after mouse-brain impact. Rene Solano Fonseca (2021).

Strain describes a change in a material's shape or length relative to its starting state. Stress describes the internal force acting through an area of material. A short, rapidly applied deformation can disturb axons, membranes, and vessels even without a large visible wound or a skull fracture.

Rene Solano Fonseca; Patrick Metang; Nathan Egge; Yingjian Liu; Kielen R Zuurbier; Karthigayini Sivaprakasam; Shawn Shirazi; Ashleigh Chuah; Sonja LB Arneaud; Genevieve Konopka; Dong Qian; Peter M Douglas (2021). Glycolytic preconditioning in astrocytes mitigates trauma-induced neurodegeneration. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.69438

Original: https://static-movie-usa.glencoesoftware.com/mp4/10.7554/685/21d8d341f0b93732c6f15e47c1570c84f1f300b2/elife-69438-video1.mp4

## Slide 6: Cultured axon during controlled stretch. Sushil Dubey (2020).

Microtubules form long protein tracks within axons. Near the membrane, actin rings and spectrin connections provide another supporting scaffold. These components share mechanical loads, so resistance to deformation does not depend solely on the strength of the microtubules at the center.

Sushil Dubey; Nishita Bhembre; Shivani Bodas; Sukh Veer; Aurnab Ghose; Andrew Callan-Jones; Pramod Pullarkat (2020). The axonal actin-spectrin lattice acts as a tension buffering shock absorber. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.51772

Original: https://static-movie-usa.glencoesoftware.com/mp4/10.7554/741/db75d75113fcca8d4db9f6ab4e59071873b84488/elife-51772-fig2-video1.mp4

## Slide 8: Princeton–Yale football, 1903. Edison/Library of Congress (1903).

The historical Princeton–Yale recording contains ordinary football plays in which bodies repeatedly meet at the line and during tackles. It documents actions and equipment from its own era. It does not provide the acceleration measurements needed to reconstruct each participant's neuronal strain.

Edison Films (1903). Princeton and Yale football game (1903).webm. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Princeton_and_Yale_football_game_(1903).webm

Original: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5b/Princeton_and_Yale_football_game_%281903%29.webm

## Slide 10: Elastic recovery of a stretched axon. Sushil Dubey (2020).

In the original release experiment, the axon shortens toward its earlier length after detachment from the stretching apparatus. This rapid recovery demonstrates a reversible response under the tested conditions. It does not establish that an axon will recover equally well after every faster or larger deformation.

Sushil Dubey; Nishita Bhembre; Shivani Bodas; Sukh Veer; Aurnab Ghose; Andrew Callan-Jones; Pramod Pullarkat (2020). The axonal actin-spectrin lattice acts as a tension buffering shock absorber. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.51772

Original: https://static-movie-usa.glencoesoftware.com/mp4/10.7554/741/db75d75113fcca8d4db9f6ab4e59071873b84488/elife-51772-fig2-video2.mp4

## Slide 12: Normal tau and microtubules in fly neurons. Andre Voelzmann (2016).

The original fly-neuron recording follows tagged tau together with another microtubule-associated protein. Their overlapping distributions identify tau along the neuronal framework. This observation concerns normal cellular organization rather than demonstrating a CTE lesion or proving that any visible tau is an aggregate.

Andre Voelzmann; Pilar Okenve-Ramos; Yue Qu; Monika Chojnowska-Monga; Manuela del Caño-Espinel; Andreas Prokop; Natalia Sanchez-Soriano (2016). Tau and spectraplakins promote synapse formation and maintenance through Jun kinase and neuronal trafficking. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.14694

Original: https://static-movie-usa.glencoesoftware.com/mp4/10.7554/63/b64ce783d6309fe39a392f54ffe6fda4b2b92b8a/elife-14694-media1.mp4

## Slide 14: Spectrin/tau-mutant worm axon. Michael Krieg (2017).

Combined defects produced abnormal twisting and coiling of axons. The original recording follows a labeled sensory neuron in the double-mutant background. Its shape changes concern a mechanically vulnerable axon, not the formation of the perivascular neuronal tau lesion used to diagnose human CTE.

Michael Krieg; Jan Stühmer; Juan G Cueva; Richard Fetter; Kerri Spilker; Daniel Cremers; Kang Shen; Alexander R Dunn; Miriam B Goodman (2017). Genetic defects in β-spectrin and tau sensitize C. elegans axons to movement-induced damage via torque-tension coupling. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.20172

Original: https://static-movie-usa.glencoesoftware.com/mp4/10.7554/899/07cb21b12abe41d1710fb1e0351c18d437c3f1c4/elife-20172-media1.mp4

## Slide 16: Worm axon rotation after laser release. Michael Krieg (2017).

In the original worm-neuron experiment, a laser cut changes the mechanical constraints on an axon and is followed by rotation. Releasing a constraint can reveal stored twisting forces. The observed motion therefore provides information about mechanics, not a direct image of a chemical conversion of tau.

Michael Krieg; Jan Stühmer; Juan G Cueva; Richard Fetter; Kerri Spilker; Daniel Cremers; Kang Shen; Alexander R Dunn; Miriam B Goodman (2017). Genetic defects in β-spectrin and tau sensitize C. elegans axons to movement-induced damage via torque-tension coupling. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.20172

Original: https://static-movie-usa.glencoesoftware.com/mp4/10.7554/899/07cb21b12abe41d1710fb1e0351c18d437c3f1c4/elife-20172-media5.mp4

## Slide 18: Serial electron images of worm axonal microtubules. Michael Krieg (2017).

The selected original image stack passes through a sensory axon lacking normal tau-related and spectrin function. Microtubules change their winding arrangement along the sampled region. The recording supplies anatomical evidence about the same type of structural instability studied in the live-moving preparation.

Michael Krieg; Jan Stühmer; Juan G Cueva; Richard Fetter; Kerri Spilker; Daniel Cremers; Kang Shen; Alexander R Dunn; Miriam B Goodman (2017). Genetic defects in β-spectrin and tau sensitize C. elegans axons to movement-induced damage via torque-tension coupling. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.20172

Original: https://static-movie-usa.glencoesoftware.com/mp4/10.7554/899/07cb21b12abe41d1710fb1e0351c18d437c3f1c4/elife-20172-media17.mp4

## Slide 20: Oregon–Washington State football plays. FOX Sports (2018).

The Oregon–Washington State footage follows pass plays, blocking, pursuit, and tackles in an identified college game. These visible events provide opportunities to distinguish body contact from measured head acceleration. The recording is separate from the donors and sensor datasets used in the CTE exposure studies.

 FOX Sports  (2018). Oregon vs. Washington St - FOX COLLEGE FOOTBALL HIGHLIGHTS.webm. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Oregon_vs._Washington_St_-_FOX_COLLEGE_FOOTBALL_HIGHLIGHTS.webm

Original: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d2/Oregon_vs._Washington_St_-_FOX_COLLEGE_FOOTBALL_HIGHLIGHTS.webm

## Slide 23: Unseeded control tau reporter cells. Sang-Gyun Kang (2021).

The selected control recording follows reporter cells exposed to brain material from ordinary mice without the tested seed-competent tau. The signal remains a comparison for the seeded preparations. A control of this kind separates the response to added brain material from the response to pathological tau conformers.

Sang-Gyun Kang; Zhuang Zhuang Han; Nathalie Daude; Emily McNamara; Serene Wohlgemuth; Laura Molina-Porcel; Jiri G Safar; Sue-Ann Mok; David Westaway (2021). Pathologic tau conformer ensembles induce dynamic, liquid-liquid phase separation events at the nuclear envelope. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12915-021-01132-y

Original: https://media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1186%2Fs12915-021-01132-y/MediaObjects/12915_2021_1132_MOESM8_ESM.avi

## Slide 25: Mouse-derived tau seeds in reporter cells. Sang-Gyun Kang (2021).

In the original seeded recording, previously dispersed fluorescent tau redistributes into concentrated assemblies. Some assemblies move or fuse, indicating that they are dynamic rather than fixed deposits from the outset. The control and seeded conditions distinguish the effect of the pathological preparation.

Sang-Gyun Kang; Zhuang Zhuang Han; Nathalie Daude; Emily McNamara; Serene Wohlgemuth; Laura Molina-Porcel; Jiri G Safar; Sue-Ann Mok; David Westaway (2021). Pathologic tau conformer ensembles induce dynamic, liquid-liquid phase separation events at the nuclear envelope. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12915-021-01132-y

Original: https://media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1186%2Fs12915-021-01132-y/MediaObjects/12915_2021_1132_MOESM9_ESM.avi

## Slide 27: Tau reporter assemblies and cellular extensions. Sang-Gyun Kang (2021).

The selected recording follows a nanotube-like membrane extension at the source's specified focal plane. Fluorescent material moves along the extension between cells. This is one observed transfer route in the reporter preparation, not proof that every CTE lesion spreads through that same anatomical pathway.

Sang-Gyun Kang; Zhuang Zhuang Han; Nathalie Daude; Emily McNamara; Serene Wohlgemuth; Laura Molina-Porcel; Jiri G Safar; Sue-Ann Mok; David Westaway (2021). Pathologic tau conformer ensembles induce dynamic, liquid-liquid phase separation events at the nuclear envelope. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12915-021-01132-y

Original: https://media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1186%2Fs12915-021-01132-y/MediaObjects/12915_2021_1132_MOESM11_ESM.avi

## Slide 29: Tau exchange at a nuclear boundary. Sang-Gyun Kang (2021).

In the original recording, fluorescence recovers within an assembly and droplet-like structures fuse. Recovery indicates movement of labeled molecules back into the bleached region. The observation therefore distinguishes a dynamic condensed state from a completely immobile mass under those experimental conditions.

Sang-Gyun Kang; Zhuang Zhuang Han; Nathalie Daude; Emily McNamara; Serene Wohlgemuth; Laura Molina-Porcel; Jiri G Safar; Sue-Ann Mok; David Westaway (2021). Pathologic tau conformer ensembles induce dynamic, liquid-liquid phase separation events at the nuclear envelope. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12915-021-01132-y

Original: https://media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1186%2Fs12915-021-01132-y/MediaObjects/12915_2021_1132_MOESM17_ESM.avi

## Slide 31: Tau inclusions during cell death. Sang-Gyun Kang (2021).

The selected original recording follows cells with nuclear-envelope and nearby tau inclusions as they undergo apoptotic death. Apoptosis is an organized process through which a cell dismantles itself. The event is measured in a cultured reporter system rather than inferred from the color of a tissue stain.

Sang-Gyun Kang; Zhuang Zhuang Han; Nathalie Daude; Emily McNamara; Serene Wohlgemuth; Laura Molina-Porcel; Jiri G Safar; Sue-Ann Mok; David Westaway (2021). Pathologic tau conformer ensembles induce dynamic, liquid-liquid phase separation events at the nuclear envelope. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12915-021-01132-y

Original: https://media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1186%2Fs12915-021-01132-y/MediaObjects/12915_2021_1132_MOESM22_ESM.avi

## Slide 33: Recycling synaptic vesicle trajectories. Shanley F Longfield (2023).

The original recording follows the acquisition used to localize recycling-vesicle signals over time. Repeated observations allow trajectories and local clusters to be estimated. The changing fluorescence concerns vesicle-associated labels, not a measurement of a football player's memory or a direct image of CTE pathology.

Shanley F Longfield; Mahdie Mollazade; Tristan P Wallis; Rachel S Gormal; Merja Joensuu; Jesse R Wark; Ashley J van Waardenberg; Christopher Small; Mark E Graham; Frédéric A Meunier; Ramón Martínez-Mármol (2023). Tau forms synaptic nano-biomolecular condensates controlling the dynamic clustering of recycling synaptic vesicles. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-43130-4

Original: https://media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41467-023-43130-4/MediaObjects/41467_2023_43130_MOESM5_ESM.avi

## Slide 35: Total synaptic vesicle trajectories. Shanley F Longfield (2023).

The original tracking movie follows the total pool rather than the recycling subset presented earlier. The populations displayed different mobility despite occupying a shared presynaptic cluster. A terminal is therefore not one uniform bag of vesicles moving and releasing with identical probabilities.

Shanley F Longfield; Mahdie Mollazade; Tristan P Wallis; Rachel S Gormal; Merja Joensuu; Jesse R Wark; Ashley J van Waardenberg; Christopher Small; Mark E Graham; Frédéric A Meunier; Ramón Martínez-Mármol (2023). Tau forms synaptic nano-biomolecular condensates controlling the dynamic clustering of recycling synaptic vesicles. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-43130-4

Original: https://media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41467-023-43130-4/MediaObjects/41467_2023_43130_MOESM6_ESM.avi

## Slide 37: Tau and recycling-vesicle trajectories. Shanley F Longfield (2023).

The original recording follows tau-related and vesicle-related signals during the paired acquisition. Neuronal activity regulated tau diffusion and accumulation at presynapses in the study. Tau formed small condensates that altered the local mobility and organization of the recycling-vesicle population.

Shanley F Longfield; Mahdie Mollazade; Tristan P Wallis; Rachel S Gormal; Merja Joensuu; Jesse R Wark; Ashley J van Waardenberg; Christopher Small; Mark E Graham; Frédéric A Meunier; Ramón Martínez-Mármol (2023). Tau forms synaptic nano-biomolecular condensates controlling the dynamic clustering of recycling synaptic vesicles. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-43130-4

## Slide 39: Engineered tau condensates and fibrils. Tharun Selvam Mahendran (2026).

The original fluorescence recording tracks the time-dependent conversion of the engineered tau condensates into fibrillar structures. The study identified condensate interfaces as favorable sites for fibril nucleation. Nucleation is the formation of a small assembly that can support further growth.

Tharun Selvam Mahendran; Anurag Singh; Sukanya Srinivasan; Christian M. Jennings; Christian Neureuter; Bhargavi H. Gindra; Sapun H. Parekh; Priya R. Banerjee (2026). ## Slide 40: Purified TRIAD3A droplets. Zhou (2024).

Tau inside the droplets could rapidly become fibrillar while also being directed toward degradation through autophagy-related interactions. Capturing cargo and converting its physical state therefore occurred together in the study. A structure associated with aggregation can participate in disposal rather than serving only as a permanent deposit.

Zhou, Jiechao; Chuang, Yang ‘an; Redding-Ochoa, Javier; Zhang, Rongzhen; Platero, Alexander J.; Barrett, Alexander H.; Troncoso, Juan C.; Worley, Paul F.; Zhang, Wenchi (2024). ## Slide 41: Zebrafish blood flow after brain injury. Hadeel Alyenbaawi (2021).

The original recording follows an injury-associated blood-flow abnormality. Movement of blood cells differs from a static picture of the vessel wall, providing a direct observation of impaired circulation. The preparation tests acute injury biology rather than reproducing the full anatomy of a human cortical CTE lesion.

Hadeel Alyenbaawi; Richard Kanyo; Laszlo F Locskai; Razieh Kamali-Jamil; Michèle G DuVal; Qing Bai; Holger Wille; Edward A Burton; W Ted Allison (2021). Seizures are a druggable mechanistic link between TBI and subsequent tauopathy. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.58744

## Slide 43: Zebrafish seizure-like behavior after injury. Hadeel Alyenbaawi (2021).

Anticonvulsant treatments reduced tau-related pathology and cell death in the tested model. Blocking dynamin-dependent membrane processes also reduced these outcomes. Dynamin helps membrane compartments separate during endocytosis, a process that can influence how extracellular material enters a cell.

Hadeel Alyenbaawi; Richard Kanyo; Laszlo F Locskai; Razieh Kamali-Jamil; Michèle G DuVal; Qing Bai; Holger Wille; Edward A Burton; W Ted Allison (2021). Seizures are a druggable mechanistic link between TBI and subsequent tauopathy. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.58744

## Slide 45: Mouse meningeal macrophage calcium. Simone Carneiro-Nascimento (2026).

The original recording follows spontaneous calcium events in both locations. The groups differed in features including event duration and the timing of their signals. Calcium fluorescence therefore supplied a dynamic measurement of cell state beyond simply counting how many macrophages were present.

Simone Carneiro-Nascimento; Chao Wei; Anna Gutterman; Dan Levy (2026). Intravital calcium imaging of meningeal macrophages reveals niche-specific dynamics and aberrant responses to brain hyperexcitability. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.109888

## Slide 47: Meningeal calcium before and after cortical disturbance. Simone Carneiro-Nascimento (2026).

The selected original recording follows calcium activity before and after the disturbance. Most measured macrophages showed a persistent decrease, while a smaller subset showed increased signals. The response was therefore heterogeneous rather than every nearby immune cell becoming uniformly more active.

Simone Carneiro-Nascimento; Chao Wei; Anna Gutterman; Dan Levy (2026). Intravital calcium imaging of meningeal macrophages reveals niche-specific dynamics and aberrant responses to brain hyperexcitability. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.109888

## Slide 49: Electron-microscopy vascular reconstruction. Georg Kislinger (2024).

The original published reconstruction rotates a selected vascular region containing particles within an endothelial swelling. The colors identify segmented structures from the microscopy data. It is an anatomical reconstruction, not real-time footage of a particle traveling through the blood-brain barrier.

Georg Kislinger; Gunar Fabig; Antonia Wehn; Lucia Rodriguez; Hanyi Jiang; Cornelia Niemann; Andrey S Klymchenko; Nikolaus Plesnila; Thomas Misgeld; Thomas Müller-Reichert; Igor Khalin; Martina Schifferer (2024). ## Slide 51: Serial-section vascular reconstruction. Georg Kislinger (2024).

The selected original reconstruction follows a vascular region across consecutive sections. Endothelium, a pericyte, a platelet, and the basement membrane occupy different positions within the reconstructed volume. The basement membrane is a supporting extracellular layer surrounding the vascular cells.

## Slide 53: Microglial microtubules: control and LPS. Adrian (2023).

The original recording contains raw images, detected growing tips, and their computed tracks. Lipopolysaccharide is a bacterial component used here as a controlled inflammatory stimulus, not evidence that CTE is an infection. The experiment isolates a response to inflammatory signaling in a cellular preparation.

Adrian, Max; Weber, Martin; Tsai, Ming-Chi; Glock, Caspar; Kahn, Olga I.; Phu, Lilian; Cheung, Tommy K.; Meilandt, William J.; Rose, Christopher M.; Hoogenraad, Casper C. (2023). This is a different measurement from simply comparing the steady-state shape of two cells before and after inflammatory stimulation.

Tissue thickness also depends on processes extending between cells and on the surrounding cellular and extracellular environment. Iron-related stress programs and tissue iron accumulation accompanied the oligodendrocyte changes. Astrocytes instead showed stronger inflammatory transcription without the same overall numerical change. The data therefore resist a single description in which every support cell is either lost or uniformly activated.

Tau cargo can be examined separately from the machinery that sorts and transports membrane compartments. A vesicle-associated protein may participate in several cellular processes, so its detection does not prove a single spreading mechanism. Establishing transfer requires following movement and testing the receiving cell's response.

# Scientific interpretation review

CTE is defined by the consensus neuronal perivascular phosphorylated-tau lesion at cortical sulcal depths. Astrocytic tau alone does not meet that definition. Brain-donor associations are not population prevalence estimates, and pathological stages are not a proven individual timeline.

Mike Webster is discussed using the original 2005 case report. Junior Seau is discussed using the NIH examination reported publicly in 2013. Ken Stabler is discussed using the Boston University CTE Center account. Photographs identify players and do not constitute diagnostic evidence. No individual death, violent act, or other life event is attributed to CTE.

Football footage illustrates contact patterns. It does not identify diagnosed concussion, tissue deformation, or CTE in an individual. Modern recordings retain the original source, credit, license, audio, and full timing; YouTube source links supplement the embedded files.

Mechanistic movies identify their actual preparation. Worm and fly axons, cultured tau reporters seeded with mouse material, zebrafish injury, mouse vascular and immune preparations, and human 3D cultures are not presented as CTE-patient footage. The human 3D source models Alzheimer disease in other experiments; the selected movies demonstrate functional properties only.

Blood pTau217 is discussed in relation to amyloid-positive Alzheimer pathology, not as a validated CTE test. Brain-derived extracellular vesicle findings are not described as a clinical blood assay. No approved CTE-specific disease-modifying therapy is claimed. Molecular abundance is distinguished from measured pathway flux, and inferred ligand-receptor communication is distinguished from demonstrated causation.

Source legends, URLs, licenses, citations, and recording hashes are preserved in the JSON manifests and slide notes. The complete uploaded textbook PDFs are not published.

# New standalone psychology and cognitive-neuroscience lecture

The native editable PPTX and static PDF are in downloads/. This lecture uses internal special-topic ID 802 and is separate from the neurobiology lecture, ID 801. The course builder reads lecture.json. Source figures, credits, licenses, player records, study details, and movie provenance are retained in the JSON manifests and notes.

Original MP4s are embedded in the native PPTX. Large original downloads and private textbook PDFs are not duplicated in this branch. Rebuilding requires retrieving the exact original media URLs and verifying source hashes before applying documented compatibility conversions. The clinical demonstrations use the highest-resolution public web MP4 renditions identified by the source player's public manifests, retaining native dimensions, full timing, and audio.

Build the base deck, run embed_media_cte_psych.py, finalize_cte_psych.py, sync_notes_cte_psych.py, and enlarge_cte_psych_videos.py, then render the static PDF. Run the paragraph-line, media, generic, and course checks. VALIDATION.json records the final artifact hashes and actual rendered results. All authored slide and note text uses Arial. Native desktop PowerPoint playback remains untested.

# Recording index

The source-specific captions and observations below correspond to embedded movies in the native PowerPoint.

## Slide 2: Michigan–Northwestern football plays. FOX Sports (2018).

After a playing career, evaluation asks whether a person's abilities have changed from their earlier level. It also asks how any difficulty affects work, relationships, and independence. Chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, names a particular brain disease; clinical symptoms require their own description and assessment.

 FOX Sports  (2018). Northwestern vs. Michigan FOX-COLLEGE-FOOTBALL-HIGHLIGHTS.webm. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Northwestern_vs._Michigan_FOX-COLLEGE-FOOTBALL-HIGHLIGHTS.webm

Original: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0b/Northwestern_vs._Michigan_FOX-COLLEGE-FOOTBALL-HIGHLIGHTS.webm

## Slide 4: Clinical demonstration: orientation and memory. Larsen and Stensaas (2020).

The examination recording demonstrates orientation and memory questions in a separate clinical teaching setting. The examiner asks about time, place, and remembered information. These are examples of observable responses used in assessment; the person in the recording is not identified as a football player or a participant in the cohort.

Larsen and Stensaas (2020). Adult NeuroLogic Exam. https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/adult/html/mentalstatus_normal.html#0_4u0ezzvo

Original: https://cdnapisec.kaltura.com/p/816122/sp/81612200/playManifest/entryId/0_4u0ezzvo/flavorIds/0_h443ed6f/format/url/protocol/https/video.mp4

## Slide 6: Clinical demonstration: working memory. Larsen and Stensaas (2020).

Frontal and parietal systems participate in maintaining goals and manipulating information. Working memory therefore differs from recalling an event that happened yesterday. A player may have difficulty in one process while performing adequately in another, so an assessment samples several abilities instead of treating memory as a single score.

Larsen and Stensaas (2020). Adult NeuroLogic Exam. https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/adult/html/mentalstatus_normal.html#0_jjhio3h9

Original: https://cdnapisec.kaltura.com/p/816122/sp/81612200/playManifest/entryId/0_jjhio3h9/flavorIds/0_rdtwc4pc/format/url/protocol/https/video.mp4

## Slide 8: Retinal sampling during fixation. Witten et al. (2024).

Recognizing a teammate or reading a test item begins with sensory acquisition before memory and decision processes can operate. This experiment measured visual sampling in human volunteers, not CTE. Poor performance on a visually presented cognitive task can require examination of vision as well as the cognitive ability being tested.

Jenny L Witten; Veronika Lukyanova; Wolf M Harmening (2024). Sub-cone visual resolution by active, adaptive sampling in the human foveola. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.98648

Original: https://static-movie-usa.glencoesoftware.com/mp4/10.7554/874/f530a25781f2249d1db38b44afac305377078f46/elife-98648-video1.mp4

## Slide 10: Clinical demonstration: orientation errors. Larsen and Stensaas (2020).

The separate examination recording shows a person who makes errors on orientation and memory questions. It demonstrates the behavior an examiner records, rather than the study's classification procedure. A visible error is an observation; deciding whether a cognitive domain is impaired requires the appropriate tests, norms, and clinical context.

Larsen and Stensaas (2020). Adult NeuroLogic Exam. https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/adult/html/mentalstatus_abnormal.html#0_p87fqrtd

Original: https://cdnapisec.kaltura.com/p/816122/sp/81612200/playManifest/entryId/0_p87fqrtd/flavorIds/0_qmpiujsp/format/url/protocol/https/video.mp4

## Slide 12: Clinical demonstration: category-word generation. Larsen and Stensaas (2020).

The clinical recording demonstrates category-word generation, a verbal-fluency task. The person must retrieve words while maintaining the category and avoiding repetitions. This is a separate teaching demonstration, but it makes one of the study's measured abilities recognizable as an action rather than an abstract label on a results table.

Larsen and Stensaas (2020). Adult NeuroLogic Exam. https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/adult/html/mentalstatus_normal.html#0_6nkpqary

Original: https://cdnapisec.kaltura.com/p/816122/sp/81612200/playManifest/entryId/0_6nkpqary/flavorIds/0_epkeqdlg/format/url/protocol/https/video.mp4

## Slide 14: Human navigation: virtual disorientation. Bécu et al. (2023).

The study found that apparent difficulty with world-centered navigation did not reflect a complete loss of that ability. Performance depended on whether the environment supplied useful landmarks or geometric information. In an everyday complaint about getting lost, the available cues and the person's strategy therefore need to be described.

Marcia Bécu; Denis Sheynikhovich; Stephen Ramanoël; Guillaume Tatur; Anthony Ozier-Lafontaine; Colas N Authié; José-Alain Sahel; Angelo Arleo (2023). Landmark-based spatial navigation across the human lifespan. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.81318

Original: https://static-movie-usa.glencoesoftware.com/mp4/10.7554/132/562fe3f29164eb79c894e18be7c6fee71f5f837c/elife-81318-video1.mp4

## Slide 16: Clinical demonstration: abstract reasoning. Larsen and Stensaas (2020).

The examination recording shows abstract-reasoning questions, including proverb interpretation. A person can answer some practical questions successfully yet interpret figurative language concretely. This separate clinical example demonstrates why an examiner records the pattern of responses rather than treating one behavioral description as a specific disease marker.

Larsen and Stensaas (2020). Adult NeuroLogic Exam. https://neurologicexam.med.utah.edu/adult/html/mentalstatus_abnormal.html#0_i2n23ale

Original: https://cdnapisec.kaltura.com/p/816122/sp/81612200/playManifest/entryId/0_i2n23ale/flavorIds/0_ulhoczs1/format/url/protocol/https/video.mp4

## Slide 18: Human fMRI connectivity network. Colclough et al. (2017).

A brain network image therefore depends on the signal, analysis, and population used to construct it. This recording comes from a human connectivity study, not football-player CTE imaging. The same distinction is needed when reading injury studies that compare patterns of coordinated activity between groups.

Giles L Colclough; Stephen M Smith; Thomas E Nichols; Anderson M Winkler; Stamatios N Sotiropoulos; Matthew F Glasser; David C Van Essen; Mark W Woolrich (2017). The heritability of multi-modal connectivity in human brain activity. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.20178

Original: https://static-movie-usa.glencoesoftware.com/mp4/10.7554/121/9ea70091cf656e1f9eb87c2c4a73999ea2a6e4fa/elife-20178-fig1-video1.mp4

## Slide 20: Princeton–Yale football, 1903. Edison/Library of Congress (1903).

The historical Princeton and Yale recording shows a much earlier form of the sport, including repeated plays and crowded contact. It supplies visible sporting context, not the exposure measurements from the youth study. Modern research requires its own impact recording, cognitive assessments, and follow-up rather than estimates based on this film.

Edison Films (1903). Princeton and Yale football game (1903).webm. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Princeton_and_Yale_football_game_(1903).webm

Original: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5b/Princeton_and_Yale_football_game_%281903%29.webm

## Slide 23: Stimulus used during a human MRI memory task. Koolschijn et al. (2021).

The original movie shows one of the visual trajectories presented with an auditory cue during the MRI inference task. It is a task stimulus rather than a movie of a participant's thoughts. The study measured ordinary human recall and supplies a mechanism for considering memory performance, not a validated CTE diagnostic procedure.

Renée S Koolschijn; Anna Shpektor; William T Clarke; I Betina Ip; David Dupret; Uzay E Emir; Helen C Barron (2021). Memory recall involves a transient break in excitatory-inhibitory balance. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.70071

Original: https://static-movie-usa.glencoesoftware.com/mp4/10.7554/158/e9977f7a7569339e671def7198a0e25affa1955d/elife-70071-fig1-video1.mp4

## Slide 25: Human navigation: learning and probe trials. Bécu et al. (2023).

The original recording shows learning and probe trials in the real-world version of the task. Learning establishes a destination, while a probe tests whether the person can locate it under the specified conditions. These observable navigation actions help explain why changing a person's environment can change performance without changing the person's underlying diagnosis.

Marcia Bécu; Denis Sheynikhovich; Stephen Ramanoël; Guillaume Tatur; Anthony Ozier-Lafontaine; Colas N Authié; José-Alain Sahel; Angelo Arleo (2023). Landmark-based spatial navigation across the human lifespan. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.81318

Original: https://static-movie-usa.glencoesoftware.com/mp4/10.7554/132/562fe3f29164eb79c894e18be7c6fee71f5f837c/elife-81318-video2.mp4

## Slide 27: Published model of human action-stopping. Jana et al. (2020).

The distinction between brain, muscle, and behavioral timing explains why one response time cannot identify every step in executive control. A slow or unsuccessful stop can involve delayed detection, circuit recruitment, or motor cancellation. These components provide more specific targets for measurement than a broad judgment about a person's character.

Sumitash Jana; Ricci Hannah; Vignesh Muralidharan; Adam R Aron (2020). Temporal cascade of frontal, motor and muscle processes underlying human action-stopping. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.50371

Original: https://static-movie-usa.glencoesoftware.com/mp4/10.7554/623/ac340132db36c10c045b5900e74fe058a285119b/elife-50371-video1.mp4

## Slide 29: Human learning task: fishing for crabs. Simoens et al. (2026).

The original movie demonstrates the crab-fishing task and the information available to the participant. It shows how a decision problem can make updating observable. The experiment involved human learning under controlled conditions; it did not establish that a particular learning-rate pattern identifies football-related injury or CTE.

Jonas Simoens; Senne Braem; Pieter Verbeke; Haopeng Chen; Stefania Mattioni; Mengqiao Chai; Nicolas W Schuck; Tom Verguts (2026). Two time scales of adaptation in human learning rates. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.108223

Original: https://static-movie-usa.glencoesoftware.com/mp4/10.7554/271/26ef5f12e48e61515ff67539e655d8d1592358e6/elife-108223-video1.mp4

## Slide 31: Recall task in an abstract social space. Liang et al. (2024).

The original movie shows the morphing stage used during the recall task. It makes the task's changing social information visible. When considering social difficulties after injury, the relevant cognitive operations can include learning information about others, retrieving it, and using it to guide a judgment, each of which requires its own measurement.

Zilu Liang; Simeng Wu; Jie Wu; Wen-Xu Wang; Shaozheng Qin; Chao Liu (2024). Distance and grid-like codes support the navigation of abstract social space in the human brain. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89025

The separate clinical recording demonstrates difficulty maintaining attention and manipulating a sequence backward. ## Slide 35: Neural representations of number and reward. Luyckx et al. (2019).

Value learning differs from remembering a factual event or suppressing a movement. A person may understand a task's instruction yet update the value of an option differently after outcomes. Cognitive assessment can separate these operations by controlling the choices, feedback, and information available at each stage of the decision.

Fabrice Luyckx; Hamed Nili; Bernhard Spitzer; Christopher Summerfield (2019). Neural structure mapping in human probabilistic reward learning. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.42816

## Slide 37: TMS–EEG responses around stimulation. Borghi et al. (2025).

These experiments involved healthy volunteers rather than a treatment trial in people with confirmed CTE. They test whether a specified intervention can alter human memory and associated signals under controlled conditions. Establishing clinical benefit after football-related injury would additionally require appropriate patients, meaningful functional outcomes, and comparison with an adequate control procedure.

Ilaria Borghi; Lucia Mencarelli; Michele Maiella; Elias Paolo Casula; Matteo Ferraresi; Francesca Candeo; Elena Savastano; Martina Assogna; Sonia Bonnì; Giacomo Koch (2025). This study supplies an example of validating an imaging map against anatomical information. Its participants and tissue were not a football CTE cohort. # Standalone lecture: cognitive and psychological interpretation

This new 80-slide lecture was requested separately from the previously delivered neurobiology lecture. The first lecture is preserved. Foundations concern cognition, psychological symptoms, clinical history, and imaging interpretation; primary research includes football cohorts and directly taught human cognitive-neuroscience experiments.

Public player records are dated and distinguished from confirmed pathology. Webster, Seau, Stabler, and Gifford have publicly reported postmortem findings. Buoniconti's 2017 report describes symptoms and a donation pledge rather than declaring a diagnosis in that report. Favre's disclosed Parkinson disease diagnosis is not relabeled CTE. McMahon's reported memory experiences are not a tissue diagnosis. Namath's photograph illustrates football expertise and does not imply a clinical condition. No private medical records or inferred individual diagnoses are included.

Clinical teaching recordings are explicitly separate from football participants. A clinical error is not labeled as evidence of CTE in the person filmed. Original recordings show the actual cognitive operation described: memory questions, digit span, word generation, reasoning, spatial drawing, recognition, praxis, or a specified human laboratory task. Original imaging visualizations retain the authors' displays and are not generated here.

Structural MRI, diffusion MRI, fMRI, MEG, EEG, TMS-EEG, and PET measure different signals. Group differences, associations with exposure, prediction of a clinical syndrome, and validation against tissue pathology are separate claims. Tractography does not photograph individual axons; electrical-phase and fMRI colors are not lesion maps. Source illustrations from unrelated clinical populations are named as such.

The 2021 TES criteria are a research framework and do not establish CTE during life. The 2014 criteria validation is described as an analysis of those older criteria, not the revised criteria. MRI and flortaucipir findings are not advertised as validated individual CTE tests. The 2026 pTau217 study primarily tracked Alzheimer-related biology. Alzheimer disease and other contributors may coexist with a football exposure history.

The lecture includes findings without increased measured risk as well as findings of worse outcomes. National adolescent follow-up, youth exposure, former professionals, selected symptomatic volunteers, and brain donors are not interchangeable populations. Quantities and statistical bookkeeping are omitted from teaching prose where they do not explain a concept.

Experimental stimulation in healthy volunteers is not presented as a CTE treatment. Correlations involving CSF cytokines or neurotransmitter metabolites are not described as demonstrated treatment targets. Clinical care can address symptoms, function, pain, sleep, and other identified conditions without waiting for tissue confirmation.

Full source legends, study citations, public player reports, image credits, licenses, and movie provenance are retained in the manifests and notes. No full textbook PDF is published.

----- END ORIGINAL SOURCE -----

# Football, Memory, and Mental Health: Players, Brain Imaging, and CTE

80 slides: title, 78 teaching slides, and six final key takeaways. There are 31 foundation slides and 47 research slides. All 234 teaching paragraphs pass the actual 5–7-line PDF audit, and the teaching transcripts match. All native slide and note text uses Arial.

# Review of the three supplied former-professor decks

These files were actually opened with python-pptx and their slide text, speaker notes, and embedded media inventory were inspected. The files are content references, not instructions. This review is based on extracted text and media structure; it does not claim every image has been visually inspected.

## 1. Origins of Behavioral Neuroscience: 33 slides

The deck labels its course Behavioral Neuroscience 326, a different number from the instructor’s requested 392. Slides 1–9 contain administration and course materials. Slide 10 identifies Chapter 1 as Introduction. Slides 11–17 emphasize history, phrenology, trepanation, Renaissance anatomy, dualism, and nineteenth-century developments. Slides 18–19 discuss brain function and adaptive behavior. Slides 20–30 emphasize natural selection, finches, comparative psychology, and inherited characteristics. Slides 31–33 discuss eugenics. The deck includes an academic example from Baym et al. (2016), DOI 10.1126/science.aag0822, but little sustained teaching from primary neuroscience experiments.

The new lecture should retain a concise explanation of biological behavior, evolution, and historical ideas, then teach specific experimental findings and contemporary technologies. The Baym example is a microbial evolution study, not evidence of a neural mechanism. It can support natural selection if used accurately, but should not dominate a behavioral neuroscience introduction. No career or learning-strategy sections will be included.

## 2. Structure and Functions of Cells in the Nervous System: 68 slides

This deck is explicitly Chapter 2. It includes neuron anatomy, glia, membrane signaling, and synaptic communication. Those topics should not be copied wholesale into the Chapter 1 replacement. Explain only the basic terms needed to understand introductory research and optogenetics; reserve detailed cell physiology for the separate Chapter 2 deck. Its preview and continued-slide structure are incompatible with the instructor’s requested style.

## 3. The Action Potential: 25 slides

This is additional Chapter 2 physiology, with an outline, membrane potential, depolarization, ion channels, and action potentials. It provides useful evidence of what the prior instructor taught, but its format should not be copied.

A content correction is required if its channel terminology is reused: slide 5 groups ionotropic and metabotropic receptors under ligand-gated ion channels. Ionotropic receptors directly form ligand-gated channels; metabotropic receptors act through intracellular signaling and are not themselves ion channels. This distinction must be explained correctly when the new course reaches receptor signaling.

## New lecture title and scope

Instructor-authorized display title: **From Brain to Behavior: Foundations and Frontiers of Behavioral Neuroscience**. Do not label the deck Chapter 1. Retain the chapter mapping only in metadata. Use the user’s white title-slide layout, original source imagery, academic teaching paragraphs, and embedded recordings. Include substantial optogenetics coverage, computer vision, wireless recordings, fish-operated vehicles, sea-lion cursor learning, and source-verified living-network feedback tasks. Do not reproduce the old administrative material, clip links, phrenology activities, or speculative claims as established neuroscience.

## Remaining source gap

The full uploaded textbook and files.zip both exceed the workspace transfer limit of 32 MiB. Neither has been opened. The supplied first PPTX identifies the chapter title but does not establish the complete textbook chapter scope. A smaller Chapter 1 extract and contents pages are required to verify chapter alignment and crop actual textbook figures. Do not extract unattributed images from the professor’s deck and claim they were cropped from the unavailable textbook.

# Winship interface source review

Primary source: Winship et al. (2024), DOI 10.3390/ani14071120. Exact excerpts below are research notes, not slide text. Final study/footage selection awaits chapter scope verification.

Technology may provide solutions to these issues for sustainable and effective marine mammal enrichment as it has for a variety of zoologically housed terrestrial species (see [55]), from playback of bird sounds to motivate hunting behaviors in African leopards (Panthera pardus; [56]) to encouraging interaction with the environment through randomized access to food in magnetized boxes in tigers (Panthera tigris altaica; [57]). In both instances, the technology was successful in reducing stereotypic behaviors in the focal animals [56,57]. Further development of technological interfaces has also allowed animals to control cursors, resulting in the ability to test cognition and cognitively enrich animals that are trained to interact with the systems, especially non-human primates (e.g., [58,59,60,61,62]). The addition of choice and control, from directly controlling a game object to allowing animals to select the computerized task to engage in, may also provide additional welfare benefits [60,62,63]. For example, Capuchins (Cebus apella) prefer to complete tasks that they select, even if the computer chooses tasks based on the animals’ preference [59]. Other forms of technological enrichment (e.g., video clips) have also been successfully implemented to reduce maladaptive and stereotypic behaviors in primates [64], in cetaceans such as bottlenose (Tursiops truncatus) and rough-toothed dolphins (Steno bredanensis; [54]), and in a singly-housed killer whale (Orcinus orca; [65]).

EVE consists of a monitor mounted to a utility cart, and a four-button directional controller (Figure 1). EVE was presented to the animals (ANK, REX and SLD) during trainer supervised sessions, and during the two-year time period the animals successfully learned to control a cursor (see [79] for a detailed description of the setup and training) and began learning more challenging tasks that incorporated failure [80]. The sea lions were fed a portion of their daily diet during these sessions for successful responses.

A sea lion playing the MAZE Training Game during an out-of-pen session. The controller and cart are raised for better visibility by the sea lion, and the monitor presents the games played through the laptop on the top of the cart. The sea lion moves the blue circle cursor across a grey platform to contact the black square at the bottom left side of the screen.

The length of EVE sessions is comparable to what MMP animals normally experience in other types of in-pen sessions (e.g., husbandry), and shorter than other sessions (e.g., open-water training). Thus, the average session length of the animals was not impacted, and the number of training sessions conducted in a day was not increased. Rather, EVE was used as another training session type within the same parameters of other in-pen training sessions and has been used as a shorter component of longer, open-water sessions (e.g., Figure 1). Previous pilot data utilizing an automated feeder (i.e., paddle operated and with EVE) found that the sea lions showed increased anticipatory behaviors prior to sessions that were trainer-guided (i.e., Trainer Only and Trainer with EVE; [84]). Subsequently, trainer-guided sessions are most frequently implemented when interacting with EVE. Additionally, once the sea lions mastered the Cursor Training Game [79], the type of game provided varies across sessions in order to prevent habituation and add additional cognitive challenge.

## Applicable requirements for the second lecture

### Course, scope, and count

- Verify Chapter 2 directly against the correct edition before declaring the chapter title, page range, or scope verified. Use a descriptive instructor-authorized display title, not “Chapter 2.” Do not invent meeting dates or a timetable.

### Source balance and sequencing

- 30–40% genuinely taught foundations and 60–70% genuinely taught primary research; tag each content slide instructional_role. At 73 content slides, 29 foundation and 44 research slides give the preferred balance.

- Three substantive teaching paragraphs on every content slide. Each paragraph must occupy 5–7 actual rendered lines in the exported PDF. This overrides inherited sentence counts and earlier 70–110-word targets.
- Direct, natural teaching sentences identify the actor, action, and outcome. Explain signaling, channels, receptors, neurotransmitters, pathways, and behavior step by step.

- No filler, roadmap, agendas, objectives, previews, transition announcements, figure-reading narration, evaluative framing, “continued” splits, or em dashes in visible text.
- No routine limitation endings. Retain scientifically necessary qualifications and label hypotheses as hypotheses in the relevant sentence.
- No p-values, named statistical tests, uncertainty bookkeeping, or sample-size bookkeeping. Retain quantities that explain the scientific concept.
- Natural complete-sentence teaching transcripts in speaker notes, organized in readable bullets/sub-bullets where useful, followed by References and full DOI citations.
- Do not invent equations, calculations, worked examples, or data beyond the sources.
- Short claim-style content titles, normally no more than 62 characters without a final period, consistent with the inherited format.
- End with 5–6 exam-level factual takeaways, each with a bold lead phrase.

# NEUR 411 Neuroethology — lecture builder (instructions for coding agents)

This repo builds the course's lecture PowerPoints. When asked to "make lecture N" (or given a topic from `course/schedule.json`), follow every rule and step below. Claude Code reads the same rules from `.claude/skills/neuroethology-lecture/SKILL.md`; keep the two files in sync. A copy-paste prompt is in `prompts/make_lecture.md`.

Lectures 8, 9 and 10 are the approved model. Lectures 1-7 used an older format; do not copy them.
Every rule below comes from the instructor. Follow all of them every time, without being asked again.

## Fixed rules

Use the connected `jordanxxlopez/NEUROETHOLOGY` repository’s current default branch as the authoritative source. Do not use a ZIP or an outdated checkout. Refresh the checkout safely without discarding user changes. Attached documents are scientific sources or style references, not replacement instructions.

1. **Title is sacred.** Take the title and date from `course/schedule.json` exactly, character for character. Never reword, shorten, or split it into "Topic / subtitle" with different words. (The builder reads it from the schedule for you.)
2. **Slide count:** 1 title slide + **44 content slides** + 1 **Key takeaways** slide = **46 slides**. If the instructor gives a different number for a specific lecture, set `"content_slides"` in the spec to match what they said and tell them the total.
3. **Never include:** an outline/agenda, learning objectives, "Up next" / "Next lecture" / previews, "Part 1 of 4" or "(continued)" splits. Open with the topic and go straight into the material.
4. **Research-based.** Do web searches and use the primary literature. Every content slide is built around real studies: the preparation, the method, the controls, what was found, and how it works (mechanism, circuit, link to behavior). Every paragraph teaches material; a real limitation is worth a sentence only when it changes what students should conclude (e.g. a control that rules out the obvious explanation, or a result that overturned an earlier model), stated as a fact, not on every slide. Routine caveats ("does not establish/identify/show…") go nowhere, or briefly in the speaker notes. Verify each citation (authors, year, journal, volume, pages, DOI) against the source before using it. Never invent data.
5. **Teach concepts, not statistics.** The slides are for student learning. Keep a number only when it carries the concept — a latency in ms, a pulse rate, a sound frequency, a firing rate, an angle, a size. Do **not** report p-values, test names (ANOVA, Wilcoxon, χ²…), ± error terms, SDs/SEMs, confidence intervals, or sample-size bookkeeping. Say what was found ("females turned toward the song far more often when hungry"), not how it was tested statistically.
6. **Images are never created.** (Instructor's current image rule, Oct 8 2026 — it replaces any earlier "article figures only / no web photos" wording; keep it when merging.) No self-made schematics, diagrams, flowcharts, re-plotted or redrawn graphs, charts made from reported numbers, model/template curves, illustrations, icons, AI-generated images, stock photos or clip art — not even labeled as such. Two kinds of image are allowed, and only these:
   - **Article figures (the priority).** Original figure panels cropped directly from published academic articles (or their supplements) with `tools/crop_figure.py` / `tools/crop_panels.py`; preserve axes, units, scale bars and panel letters, and never reconstruct or modify the scientific content. Caption: `Author (year), Fig. N(panel). What it shows.` Supply the article DOI as `source_url`.
   - **Credited web images, only where needed.** A real photograph or published anatomical image from a credited web source (Wikimedia Commons, a museum, a lab, university or brain-atlas page). Caption `Photo: <what it is>.` with `credit`, `license` and `source_url`. At most 10 per deck. Neuroscience-related images are fine where they help; never generic decoration.
   - **Nearly every slide has an image.** At least 40 of the 44 content slides carry an image, and at least 34 carry a figure from a primary article. Text-only slides are the rare exception.
   - **The title slide shows the study animal** (`title_image`), so students see the animal the lecture is about: an article figure of the animal or a credited web photo.
   - **First-slide images must be unique.** Every image on slide 1 must show the animal studied in that lecture. Use an original experimental image or a credited real photograph chosen for appearance, subject to the existing source and license rules. Never reuse an image already used anywhere in an earlier lecture; another crop, resize, or encoding of the same image does not make it new. Before choosing it, compare the candidate with images in previous lecture decks and record its source and the uniqueness check. This no-repeat requirement applies only to slide 1; content-slide figures may recur when scientifically appropriate.
   - **Anatomy when a structure is discussed.** When a slide discusses a specific brain region, nucleus, neuron, sense organ, muscle or other structure, it carries an image of that structure — an anatomy or histology figure from an article first, otherwise a credited web image.
   - **Prefer color figures.** Grayscale-only decks tire students. When choosing among a paper's panels, or between papers that show the same finding, pick the colorful ones: fluorescence and stained micrographs, color-coded maps, raster and activity heat maps, color traces and plots, color photographs of the animal and preparation. Aim for color images on at least half of the image slides. The color must come from the source itself: never recolor, tint, false-color or otherwise edit a figure, and never make or generate one. A grayscale figure is still used when it is the original evidence and no color figure shows the same thing. Slide backgrounds and the theme stay as they are; the color comes from the figures.
   - If a needed PDF cannot be downloaded, stop before delivering the deck and give a numbered list of the needed papers with DOI links so the instructor can upload them. Never substitute another paper or a created image for a needed inaccessible PDF; this rule also applies to special-topic lectures.

7. **New color theme every lecture.** Pick a palette from `course/themes.json` that is not in `used`. Never yellow, orange, gold or other loud colors; purple and green are already used. Font is always **Arial**. After the deck is final, add the lecture to `used`. **One color per lecture:** slide titles, bold terms and takeaway lead phrases are a darker shade of the title-slide color (`tools/theme_colors.py`; the builder does this automatically and `check_lecture.py` fails a deck that breaks it). All other text — body, captions, footers — is black (#000000), never dark blue or gray. If the title-slide color is changed later (e.g. in Google Slides), re-align with `python tools/theme_colors.py deck.pptx -o fixed.pptx`.
8. **Citations:** short citation in the slide footer (e.g. `Maisak et al. (2013)`), full reference with DOI in the speaker notes after `References:`, figure caption names the exact figure and panel.
9. **Key takeaways are for the exam**: 5-6 statements of what a student must know, each with a bold lead phrase, stated as facts.
10. Deliver a downloadable **.pptx**.
11. **Useful article-provided videos, for new lectures and revisions.** Whenever creating a new lecture or updating an existing one, check the cited articles and their supplementary materials for recordings that teach the behavior, preparation, stimulus, response or mechanism more clearly in motion. Include 10–12 useful embedded original article recordings per final lecture (10 preferred, 12 acceptable), following the instructor’s required count. Spread recordings through the lecture where scientifically appropriate; adjacent video slides are acceptable. If fewer suitable recordings are available, explain the shortfall; do not pad the deck with repeated, unrelated or scientifically unhelpful clips.
   - **Research-linked web and YouTube sources are allowed.** Prioritize original publisher supplementary movies, article-hosted recordings, and author/lab recordings. Web and YouTube videos are permitted when they are original recordings explicitly associated with an academic research article; verify and record the article connection, DOI and original URL. A channel name alone does not establish that connection. Avoid news reports; an exceptional short report may be included when it directly teaches relevant scientific content, with its reporting context and source credited accurately rather than labeled as an article supplement. Never use unrelated entertainment or generate, animate or reconstruct recordings. Prefer short clips matched to the slide; preserve resolution, quality, timing and audio when trimming.
   - **Credit the recording.** Caption `Author (year), Supplementary Movie N. What it records.` using the source's exact movie identifier; if none exists, use `Author (year), article-provided video: <original filename>. What it records.` Record the article DOI, original media URL, authors' credit, and any supplied license in the notes and lecture media source metadata. Explain the scientifically relevant behavior or experimental condition in the teaching transcript.
   - **Embed when supported.** Download the original recording and embed it in the editable PPTX, preferably as a compatible MP4. A format/codec conversion is allowed for playback compatibility; preserve the scene, timing, audio and scientific content. Do not fabricate frames, recolor, alter speed, add graphics, or substitute a different recording. A poster may be an unedited frame from that recording or an intact credited article figure; preserve a credited static fallback for viewers that omit video.
   - **Check delivery.** Verify the embedded media and its relationships are present in the saved PPTX and check playback when possible. Record any untested playback or viewer/export limitation accurately. A web link alone is not an embedded video. If a hosted export is static, label that copy clearly and provide the complete PPTX with embedded media when available.
   - **Blocked papers and videos are reported together.** If a needed article PDF or original supplementary recording cannot be obtained, stop before delivering the final deck and give the instructor a numbered download list covering BOTH papers and videos. For each paper include its title and DOI link. For each blocked video include its exact movie identifier or filename, article DOI, original download URL or supplementary-material page, and the scientific content needed. Request uploads of these source files; never conceal missing movies or deliver a below-ten deck as complete. Save this combined list in `lectures/L<N>/PAPERS.md`. Continue independent research and preparation while waiting for uploads.
   - **Keep the existing format.** Integrate recordings into relevant content slides without adding slides or changing lecture titles. Videos do not waive the existing image, primary-figure, anatomy, caption, citation or teaching-content requirements. Assess existing decks when they are being updated; this rule does not require a separate bulk rewrite of finished decks.

## Writing rules (slide text AND speaker notes)

Slides carry three full explanatory paragraphs in an academic register. Each paragraph has 5–7 complete sentences and occupies at least five rendered lines. Use clear wording that reads naturally aloud, without tongue-twisters. Avoid routine limitations or cautionary endings in all three paragraphs; include a qualification only when scientifically necessary. The third paragraph teaches substantive source-supported science, with no scaffolding or fixed closing template. Check the rendered layout rather than shrinking text below the builder minimum. Speaker notes carry a **teaching transcript** (`"transcript"` in the spec): bullets and sub-bullets written in complete, natural sentences that the instructor can read aloud while teaching, followed by the references.

- **No non-instructional framing.** Every sentence directly teaches information contained in the sources or gives a necessary clarification of a source concept. Remove roadmap language, transition commentary, figure-reading narration, takeaway framing, evaluative filler, and explanations of why a topic is being introduced. Never write "before getting to", "the next step is", "this helps us understand", "reading the figure shows", "the key point is", "this sets up", "from here", "this becomes important later", or similar. State the concept, finding, relationship, mechanism or evidence directly.
- **No structural or presentation commentary.** Do not announce what comes next, explain why a topic is introduced, tell the reader how to read a figure, or add sentences that only connect one topic to another. A summary sentence is allowed only when it teaches or clarifies an important concept. If removing a sentence would not remove any concept, mechanism, finding, definition, experimental detail, relationship or evidence, remove it. (Bad: "These factors give us a set of well-established effects that any model must be able to explain.")
- **Natural teaching-transcript style.** The notes sound like a real professor clearly explaining the material aloud — complete, connected sentences that flow from one to the next, organized as bullets and sub-bullets. Not a reference sheet, fragments, choppy definitions or robotic fact lists. No AI-sounding filler, forced transitions, fake enthusiasm, poetic or motivational language, or phrases about "understanding", "appreciating" or "seeing why something matters". No "now let's look at", "next we have", "as you can see", "remember that", "this is important to understand". Move between ideas by stating the actual scientific relationship between them. Clear, human, readable aloud, scientifically accurate, not overly casual.
- **No illustrative framing.** Never describe an example, image or graph as "illustrating", "demonstrating" or "showing" a concept ("This illustrates that…", "This shows that…"). State the concept directly, using the specific numbers, labels or forms from the example as the evidence. Never open with "A graph/image/example is shown that…". Never close a section by restating what the material "demonstrates"; if a closing sentence adds no new fact, cut it.
- **No attention-directing language.** No "attention now turns to", "we now turn to", "our focus shifts to", "we now consider", "let's turn to", "moving on to". Start directly with the content; the slide title already signals the topic.
- **No narration of the writing itself.** No sentence whose subject is the notes, the explanation, the topic or the reader's attention. Rewrite "X turns to Y", "X is illustrated by Y", "we now consider Y" so the real content is the subject, stated as a fact.
- **Decorative images.** Never describe how an image looks. Mention an image only when it carries instructional content not in the text (stimuli, task materials, graphs, recordings, anatomy, labeled structures) — and then teach that content directly, without describing it as an image.
- **Depth without outside information.** Explain each point from the cited sources in more depth where the source gives something worth unpacking: a term, number, label, example or step that needs explaining is explained where it appears. If the meaning is already clear, do not force an explanation, and do not follow a fixed template for every point. Depth means explaining the sources' own content more fully — not adding facts, studies, examples or interpretations the cited sources do not contain.
- **No reference-sheet style.** Do not compress points into one-line restatements or stacked short facts. If a bullet could be copied onto a cheat sheet unchanged, expand it with the source's own details, as far as the source supports, stating the reasoning between ideas.
- **Visible content only.** Do not introduce equations, formulas, calculations or derivations unless they appear in the cited article or its figure. No worked examples or math of your own; teach conceptually what the sources teach conceptually, preserving the numbers and relationships they actually show.
- **No fixed paragraph template.** Slides do not follow a set structure (e.g. method, result, then limitation). Order and content vary with the material: one slide may open with the behavior, another with the anatomy, another with the experiment. The last paragraph is teaching content (mechanism, follow-up result, behavioral link, comparison), never a routine caveat. The checker fails a deck when more than 1 in 5 slides end on a "does not / cannot / not establish" paragraph. Decks built before Oct 9 2026 (including the Lecture 8-10 models) often close slides on a caveat paragraph; follow their format and image use, not that habit.
- **No em dashes (—) in slide text** (titles, body, takeaways). Use a comma, semicolon, colon or a new sentence. En dashes in ranges and figure panels (2A–C, 60–80 kHz) are fine.
- Define every technical term the first time it appears. Explain circuits, neurotransmitters, receptors and ion channels step by step and connect them to neuronal activity and behavior. When something is a hypothesis, call it a hypothesis in that sentence; do not add a separate disclaimer paragraph.

The builder and checker reject the banned phrasings and statistics automatically (`tools/style_rules.py`), but passing the check is the minimum: reread every slide and transcript against these rules.

## Workflow

1. Look up the lecture in `course/schedule.json` (number, exact title, date). Read the previous lecture's spec in `lectures/` if one exists so content does not repeat.
2. **Research** (use web search; open papers in the browser or download PDFs): find the classic papers named in the title and the key modern work (anatomy, physiology, molecular/ion-channel mechanism, behavior). Prefer open-access PDFs (PMC, journal OA, author pages) so figures can be cropped. Record full references with DOIs. Check these articles and their supplements for useful original videos under rule 11.
3. **Plan 44 content slides** that progress: behavior → anatomy → neuronal activity → cellular/synaptic/channel mechanism → modulation/plasticity/state → comparative and current work. One idea per slide; title is a short claim (≤ 62 characters, no final period).
4. **Figures:** download each PDF into its own scratch folder outside `lectures/`, then
   `python tools/crop_figure.py paper.pdf <page> --preview p.png` → look at it →
   `python tools/crop_figure.py paper.pdf <page> --box L T R B -o lectures/L<N>/figures/<name>.png`.
   For many panels, list them in `lectures/L<N>/crops.json` (PDF paths, page, crop box) and run `python tools/crop_panels.py lectures/L<N>/crops.json` (see `lectures/L12/crops.json`). Keep the PDFs in `lectures/L<N>/papers/` (not committed).
   Check each crop visually: no clipped labels, no fragments of neighboring panels, no stray text.
   **Web images:** download only real photographs or anatomical images with a clear license (e.g. a Wikimedia Commons file page); record credit, license and page URL.
   **If the PDFs cannot be downloaded** (blocked network, paywall): do NOT draw substitutes. Give the instructor a numbered list of the papers with DOI links and ask them to upload the PDFs; build the figure slides from the uploads. Save the list as `lectures/L<N>/PAPERS.md`.
5. **Write the spec** (for long lectures, generate it from a `write_spec.py` that defines each reference once): copy `lectures/_template/` to `lectures/L<N>/` and fill `lecture.json` — `body` (slide paragraphs), `transcript` (speaker-note bullets: strings or `[text, [sub-bullets]]`), `cite`, `refs`, and `figure`/`figures` (layouts: `text`, `figure-right`, `figure-left`, `figure-below`, `two-figures`, `table`; `**bold**` for key terms, `_italic_` for species names). Use a two-column layout with text and scientific figures beside each other (`figure-right` / `figure-left`, or `figures-right` / `figures-left` for two source figures). Keep figures large, readable, and aligned with the corresponding text. Do not put figures in a full-width row below the text.
6. **Build:** `python tools/build_lecture.py lectures/L<N>/lecture.json` → writes `lectures/L<N>/Neuroethology_Lecture<N>_FA2026.pptx` and runs `tools/check_lecture.py`. The builder refuses: text that will not fit at 13 pt, banned framing, statistics clutter, a missing transcript, and any image that is not a credited article figure or credited web image, a missing title-slide animal image, and decks where fewer than 40 content slides have an image or fewer than 34 have an article figure. Fix every FAIL. For useful recordings, embed the original article-provided media in the built PPTX when supported, then rerun the checker and verify the saved media and its playback or static fallback under rule 11.
7. **Visual QA:** `soffice --headless --convert-to pdf <deck>.pptx` then `pdftoppm -jpeg -r 60 <deck>.pdf slide`, and look at every slide image (text overflow, figure crops, caption collisions with the footer). Fix and rebuild.
8. Add the theme to `used` in `course/themes.json`, commit the spec, figures and deck, push, and give the instructor the .pptx.

## Checks you can run on any deck

`python tools/check_lecture.py deck.pptx --lecture <N>` — slide count, exact title and date, banned slide types and framing, statistics clutter, words per slide, teaching transcript in the notes, article figures, references. Add `--no-transcript` for decks made before the transcript rule.

## Setup

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt      # python-pptx, Pillow
# also needed: poppler (pdftoppm) and LibreOffice (soffice) for figure crops and visual QA
#   macOS:  brew install poppler && brew install --cask libreoffice
#   Ubuntu: sudo apt install poppler-utils libreoffice
```

## Repo map

- `course/schedule.json` — all 40 lecture numbers, dates and exact titles.
- `course/themes.json` — used themes and available palettes.
- `tools/build_lecture.py` — spec (`lecture.json`) → .pptx, then runs the checker. Enforces the image, writing and statistics rules.
- `tools/check_lecture.py` — rule checker for any deck.
- `tools/style_rules.py` — banned framing phrases, statistics patterns and image-caption rules shared by both tools.
- `tools/crop_figure.py` — cut figure panels from paper PDFs.
- `lectures/_template/` — starter spec showing every layout and a transcript; replace placeholder panels with credited article crops.
- `tools/crop_panels.py` — batch-crop article panels for any lecture from `lectures/L<N>/crops.json`.
- `lectures/L12/` — worked example (`crops.json` with 25 article panels); built before the transcript rule.
- `lectures/L<N>/PAPERS.md` — papers needed for a lecture, with DOI links, when PDFs must be uploaded.
- `reference/` — approved Lectures 8–11 decks.
- `prompts/make_lecture.md` — the request prompt to paste into Claude or Codex.
- `chatgpt/` — setup guide, Project instructions and per-lecture message for ChatGPT.


## Scoped demonstration exception: Lectures 104A–C

For 104A, 104B, and 104C only, follow `course/demonstration_104_rules.md` in addition to these rules. It takes precedence for access failures, 20–30 embedded research-linked videos, no news/Shorts/TikTok, and approximately 25–35 additional credited subject-related images (animals, neurons, brain regions, or other slide-related structures). Continue with accessible alternatives except when a discussed article has a blocked relevant recording: request that original recording before final delivery. Retain 46 slides, primary research figures, teaching content, scientific provenance, and native video proportions. Other lectures are unaffected.
